We beg leave to direct attention to the article, which we have copied from the Illustrated London News, on Post Office Accommodation, and especially to the words which we have placed in Italics, as containing an idea particularly remarkable, and we are bold to say, quite new to our community. The light in which the press is viewed by constitutional and by absolute Governments presents so remarkable a difference, that, in the one case, it may well be called þÿ a branch of the public service while, in the other case, unless it be truly a branch of the Government sendee i. e. a mere þÿ tool and flatterer of the Governmentþÿ its success is doubtful ; but its extinction sure. When we compare our situation with that of the neighbouring British Islands,

society, with its mixed races, the one predominant and the other subordinate, at the same degree of advancement in intelligence and civilization, we are disposed to regret our hard lot, that while they possess not occur all the blessings which a free, legislative government and an unshackled press can confer, we are told (and alas ! there are but too many who find it for their interest to believe it) that we are yet unprepared þÿ for such institutions ! ! Vredat Judaus !

We rejoice in being able to report that the Island has, within the last few days, been blessed with seasonable and refreshing showers. With a continuation of such weather and high prices we may feel some degree of confidence in the future.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE SLAVE TRADE. þÿ BRAZIL. Mr. Roebuck called the attention of the House to the subject of our relations with Brazil, and moved for a Select Committee to take into consideration those relations, and to report thereupon. The hon- and learned member, in supporting his motion, contended that the Brazilian Government had done all in its power to extinguish the slave trade, in accordance with the spirit of its treaties with this country ; that the longer interference of our cruisers with Brazilian vessels was altogether unnecessary, while it was offensive to the dignity of the Brazilian Government, and detrimental to the interests of Brazilian commerce. Ho therefore asked fora Committee iu order that it might be ascertained whether it would not bo wise to put our relations with that country upon a different footing, and upou a good understanding with a country with

s T-, eilll «\ v ti a, which we had such extensive commercial connections. Mr. B. Moore seconded the motion. Lord Palmerston opposed the motion, as bring entirely uncalled for. Ho asserted that the cruisers of this country bad done nothing more than was necessary to suppress the slave trade, and that the statements made by Mr Roebuck with reference to our interference with Brazilian commerce were considerably exaggerated. He accused that gentleman of having yielded to vulgar and unfounded insinuations when he asserted that this country bullied the weak and succumbed to the powerful. In conclu-ion, he called upon the House to reject a motion the adoption of which would give encouragement to slave-dealers, and tend to the extension of the slave trade in all directions ('Cheers). Mr. M Milnes urged Mr. Roebuck to withdraw his motion, not because there was no ground for inquiry, but because it would be quite useless to go to a division upon it. Mr. Roebuck, iu reply, charged Lord Palmerston with aiding and assisting the strong, such as the Governments of Spain and America, and bullying the weak, such as the Government of Brazil. He declined to withdraw his moliou. Mr Disraeli admitted the importance of the subject, and thought the House was much indebted to Mr. Roebuck for bringing it forward. At the same time he declined to support the motion, believing the appointment of a Select Committee to be unnecessary and too strung a measure for the occasion. Lord J. Russell recommended that the matter

should be left in the hands of the Government, whose management of our diplomatic relations ought to satisfy the House. The House then divided, when the numbers were þÿ For Mr. þÿRoebuck s motion, 17 ; against 312: majority, 295. The motion was therefore lost.

An official notification in the Berliner St, ants Anzeiger followed by statements in both Houses of the British Parliament, has made known during the week the betrothal of the Princess Royal of Great Britain, and, in right of her father, Duchess of Saxony, to his Royal Highness the Prince Frederick William, nephew of the present King of Prussia, and son of the heir apparent to the Prussian throne. The event will excite in the minds of the people of Great Britain the same nffectionat loyalty which was expressed with such graceful unanimity by all parties in the British Legislature, and has already been hailed by the Protestant people of Prussia with a satisfaction closely bordering upon enthusiasm. At the time at which we write no notification has been m d. of the amount of provision which Parliament will be called upon to make for the Princess in this important crisis of her life ; but, whatever differences of opinion may be called into existence on this point, the generous British people, heavily taxed as they are, will cordially apfirove of a liberal allowance. to that flourishing monarchy will, probably, find it as consistent with his public dignity as wit , his personal feelings to deprecate any allowance which would seem to make him appear, in the eyes of his own people as well as in those of the countrymen and countrywomen of his future Queen, to be a pensioner upon the bounty of a foreign country. The numerous piogeny with which Heaven has blessed the Queen of England affords so many securities f >r the lineal transmission of the British Crown in the male line that it may perhaps appear ungracious to hint that, v\ hen British Princesses marry the lieiis to Continental thrones, it would be politic to exclude them and their children from the chances, which might otheiwise be theirs, of succession to the British Crown Yet we scarcely think such exclusion unnecessary. If the direct male descendants of her Majesty should fail, and the right of succession should d scend to the female line, it would lie unfortunate, and might lead to many troubles, if the heir to the British Crown should happen to be at the same time King of Prussia or Emperor of Austria or Russia. The proud kingdom of England could not tolerate the idea of being an appanage to any ol the powerful monarchies of the Continent ; and it should be the business of a wise Legislature to guard against su h a danger, however, remote it may appear. By a policy which many sensible and 1 >yal people think to be unwise, if not unnatural, the Princesses of England are forbidden to

marry among their own countrymen. Tha danger guarded against in this case is that of raising up aristocratic families too nearly related to the Crown to peifoim the duties of ordinary citizens ; hut the danger, remote, though possible, resulting from alliances with the Sovereigns of Europe ought to be guarded against with as much, or even greater, care. The time has come when the marriages of her Maþÿjesty daughters, s following in due course, the one after the other, will force this subject upon the attention of Parliament and the public ; and there can be no time more propitious for its dispassionate consideration than a time when the male succession is apparently well secured in the person of his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales and of thne other Princes. This question is, in fact, a far more important one than that of dowry or allowance on which so many of the public journals have permitted themselves to indulge in extravagant and unwarranted speculations ; but, as it does not so immediately touch the feelings þÿ or rather the þÿpockets of the people, has been almost, if not altogether, lost sight of, except by the few advanced minds who have studied history. The satisfaction of the British people at the severance of their political and dynastic connection with Hanover was great and well founded. That connection led the nation into many difficulties, dangers, and expenses, from the effects of which it is still suffering. If true wisdom con-ists in being warned by the experience of

the past, true wisdom should dictate to the Legislature at the present time the necessity of avoiding the recurrence of similar entanglements ; which, in such a case as that of Prussia, or any other leading State of Europe, would be far woise than with a small S;ate like II nover. For considerably upwards of a century the question lias not arisen j but, having arisen in 1857, it must be fairly met and duly considered.

THE BELGIAN ULTBAMONTANE8. TO THE EDITOR OF THE TIMES. Sir, þÿ Amid the din and bustle of your general elections events have occurred in Belgium 'which, though hitherto disregarded in England, are calculated to exercise a momentous influence on the future of that country. In order that your readers may understand the nature of the present crisis let me recur for a moment to the occurrences of 1848. Prior to the French Revolution of February parties were pretty equally balanced in the Belgian Legislative Assembly, the Liberals and Ultramoutanes having alternately a small majority, rarely exceeding six or eight. The Revolution found Belgium in possession of a Liberal Ministry, and, thanks to the wisdom of the King, the prudence of the Government, and the loyalty of the people, the country passed safely through the storm which levelled nearly every other continental Government. Then came the reaction in France and elsewhere þÿ a reaction of which the Ultramontane party was not slow to avail itself. The franchise being on a most extended scale, the great majority of voters in the villages and country districts, more particularly in the Flemish provinces, arc profoundly ignorant and completely under the domination of the priests Called on to exercise the elective franchise they are driven by the cure in flocks, like sheep, to the poll in the full belief that Liberals, Freemasons, and Atheists are synonomous terms, for so are they taught hebdomadally. The intelligent populations of Brussels, Antwerp, Liege, and Verviers have struggled in

vain against this priestly domination, and some two or three years ago the Ultramontane party obtained a decided majority in the Legislative Assembly. The King, who thoroughly understands his position as a constitutional monarch, was compelled to form a Government the opinions of which were in accordance with those of the Parliamentary majority. The Liberal ministry was dismissed, and that of M. de Decker, a mere tool of the priests, appointed in its place. No sooner was this triumph gained than intolerance and bigotry assumed new developments. The most able organs of the press protested in vain. The bishops replied let- by were kept in readiness, artillery was stationed excommunicating thuir readers. Pastoral ters were issued warning parents of the fate which awaited those who (lid not patronize the Jesuit College of Louva: ., and the State Universities of Ghent and Liege were put under episcopal ban. At length the peir seemed i ripe, and about two mouths back the Government introduced the Bill upon Charitable Institutions, which was the immediate cause of d' last þÿweek rioting. s The administration of charity in Belgium ince 1830 has been completely secularized and concentrated in the hands of the civil power. Religious congregations and members of the clergy of every denomination are legally incapable receiving distributing of or alms and bequests destined for the poor. '1 his distribution is made by two intsitutions specially appointed for the purpose þÿ the Administrations

Llospitalieres and the Bureaux de Bienfaisanu All bequests to religious congregations are null and void, and all donations in favour of the poor are remitted to the abovenamed institutions. It will thus be seen that Belgium enjoys a law more limited in its application than our Law of Mortmain, but still atfording a protection against the priest to the dying þÿ citizen and his family. The Ministerial Bill proposes that the Go vernment shall have the power, by a simple decree under the þÿKing hand, s of conferring on j religious congregations the rights of citizens, with all the privileges attaching thereto, inreceiving all donations and legacies given or and sittings cluding those of possessing, inheriting, and the bequeathed to them. On the other hand, they who wish to dispose of their fortune in favour of the poor, or for charitable purposes, will have tlie right to name special administrators of such property as they shall devote to that j acted at Antwerp, Mens, Liege, and Ghent. end. In fact, the proposed Bill practically repeals the existing laws, and withdraws all protection from the dying man, whom it leaves in the hands and at the mercy of his spiritual attendant. But, this is not all. It is fraught with danger to the Crown, for a family disinherited in favour

T- HOIK A V IS.. of a convent will bear no goodwill towards the King who has þÿs gned the decree wh reby that convent is rendered capabl of inheriting, and whereby they are ruined þÿ We have liberty of þÿspeech, say the Ministers and the priests, þÿ liberty of the press, liberty of meeting; let us, then, have liberty of charity þÿ! However, the Bili was brought in, ar.d the discussions were, regarded with the gr atest anxiety by the public, who crowded the Tribunes daily. T e debates lasted upwards of a month, and on the 19th ult. the principle of the bill was affirmed by a majority of 60 to 44, one member declining to vote, and five only being absent. A noble stand was made during the whole discussion by Messrs. Rogier, Verhaegen, Orts, Tesch, and Frcre-Orban, who fought tlie ground inch by inch, shivered the feeble arguments of their opponents, arid were beaten only by force of numbers. The principle of the Bill being carried the Opposition proposed amendment after amendment. Continually defeated, they were ever at their post, supported by the great mass of the þÿcountry intelligence. s The applause wherewith their speeches were greeted from the tribunes roused the ire of the Ministeriali-ts, who declared that the Assembly was deliberating under duresse, and three times dun ig the debates were the tribunes chared by force At length, on Wednesday last, M. Frere- Orban, having declared that the Government were playing an u indig tie comedie" before the Chamber and the country, wa< called to order

by the President. He at on e replied by acþÿ cusing the infame þÿ having been applied to him by a President of partiality, the word member on a previous occasion, and passed uncensured by the President. This sally was received with immense applause in the tribunes, and the President ordered them to he cleared forthwith. Amid the groans and yells of the occupants this task was slowly effected by the gendarmes. The crowd then rushed outside the Chamber and hooted the þÿPope s Nuncio. They yelled at the Ministers, cheered the Opposition members, and in the evening paraded the town in groups of 50 or 60. Next evening they broke the windows o. the Emancipation office, a journal specially devoted to the priest party, and likewise those of the Jesuits and other religious establislnn nts. The troops

on the Grande Place, and great excitement prevailed. On Friday the Burgomaster issued a proclamation forbidding groups of more than five to assemble, and in the evening the mounted gendarmes dispensed those who endeavoured to evade its effect. Yesterday tlie King published a decree proroguing the Chamber sine \ an !, in all probability, the Ministerial Bill will be heard of no more. Meanwhile riots have occurred at Mona and at Antwerp, at Ghent, and at L:ege The old spirit is roused among the burghers, and they seem determined to resist any further attempts at priestly domination. The resolution adopted by the King is the wisest that could be taken under the eircumst;.; ce.s. It will probably restore j < ice and order, by giving the Government an opportunity of quietly dropping their obnoxious measure without the appearance of yielding to public clamour. Would that tlie pr csts could profit by the lesson, but, like the Bourbons, they learn nothing and forget nothing. I remain, Sir, yours obediently. AN ENGLISH RESIDENT IN BELGIUM. May 31.

The flames had already gained the roof when the terrible fact was announced by the ringing of the bells. The inhabitants transported themselves with all imaginable promptitude to the scene of disaster, and contributed their utmost efforts with heroic courage, not to save the Pharmacy, which was already completely embraced by the flames, but at least to concentrate them there, and to prevent, if possible, their spread. These efforts, however, wore useless ; the fire fed by a North North East wind, propagated itself with extraordinary rapidity, never arresting itself either by the hou-es which it destroyed, nor by water. constant exercise of 6 pumps furnishing the In less than 6 hours five squares or ilets, and ninety three houses, became a prey to the flames in our unfortunate town, so subject to

$ these calamities. On the present occasion, j ihe devastation partieulirly embraced the richest quarter of the town where the highest commercial transactions were held. The progress of the tire was only arrested to the Eastward, | by t!.e market place and the street of Frontsforts, and to the West by the sea, after consuming all the deposits of wood and lumber which happened to be on the quay. The Cus- l torn House has been spared. Thus the im- i mense square contained between the Main Street (Grand rue), the street of Bonne-foi, the j more to the view at present but an immense Quay, and the street Traversiere, otfer nothing j ! mound of ashes and yet smoking ruins. It is impossible to estimate the enormous extent of the losses sustained by the proprietors, or of those accruing to commerce. Merchandize, which had been extracted from the stores and transported to distant places of imagined safety, were burnt in the streets, and in those very places where they were considered free of danger. Never was there a more cruel, nor a more horrible spectacle presented to the eye, than that of this immense flame raised up as if it were all at once over this vast quarter þÿ never a spectacle more afflicting than that seen by a large portion of our unfortunate population, and signed by a large majority of people who, were imploring the Mercy of God with uplifted hands, from whom alone they hoped the question of county annexation submitted for efficacious þÿsuccour whilst giving their as-

sistance to stop the ravages of the iiames. The Emperor was among the foremost in presenting himself at the different points which were in flames. His Majesty manifested on this sad event the utmost energy. He gave all the orders himself, and saw that they were executed He transported himself to these points with much solicitude, and seemed to be present everywhere at the same time. This personal devotion on the part of the Chief of the State, sustained the courage of everybody, and communicated to all a noble and heroic ardour. Citizens were seen on the tops of the roofs, axe in hand, surrounded by fire, disputing with the fire its prey, and who only left off, as we may say, when their skin began to be scorched by it; others were to be seen precipitating announces but one case of fever, and that very themselves at the peril of their lives into the interior of houses already in flames, drawing from within poor women in despair, senseless, who had fast hold of the furniture, and had given themselves up to what appeared their Thus far the experiment has succeeded beyond fate. Throughout the whole throng, and amongst moters. all ranks, were remarked heroic traits of courage and generous devotion. We give an instance : The Emperor had given orders to pull down a house contiguous to another in llames. They approach with eagerness, they hesitate, they draw back, the heat of the fire causing them to dread the danger. The Colonel commanding the execution of the order then sprung forward, climbed the roof, and

went axe in hand almost into the midst of the flame, the whole of the officers pres nt, and a number of citizens, imitated this fine example, and in a twinkling the house was demolished. Honor to Colonel Pierre Mnrassa. It gives us pleasure to tender our homage to the Ministers for their activity and devotion, to the Grand Chancellor, and to the Count of I'etion Ville, Governor of the capital. They have obtained a great portion of admiration. In our next number will be cited the names of those who signalized themselves in this unhappy night. Our desire is to give to each the praise which is merited. The loss of two victims is to be deplored ; one of whom, a clerk of the administration, precipitated himself into the flames, and was suffocated by the smoke and heat ; his body was brought forth before it was burnt. Another individual was entirely consumed in a house. This unfortunate man was seen at a dormitory window making the most frantic gestures, which were nor comprehended, neither could he be heard ; they hailed to him to come down as they were ignorant that the interior was on fire. Finally, in a wild manner he came quickly from the dormitory window, followed Bhort time disappeared with him in the midst of a vortex or whirlwind of flame. Natives and foreigners, if they do not all equally avouch the fact, prove it either positively or negatively, whatever derangement in our social economy may result from the discovery in our immediate neighbourhood of such an attraction to our laboring hands, and it is no use to attempt any longer " to pluck the flower safely from the nettle to conceal it. We must therefore try

over a wider field, diminish the pressure of the attraction upon our own population. With this object I send you a letter which I received from an agent whom I sent up to the diggings to get information and to try his luck if there

Extract from, letter dated Cuidad Tinlivar , 2nd July 1852. Air. Elias Gorrin. Dear Sir, þÿ The samples of gold which you now take with you, come from the. lliver Yuruary. That river runs nearly West to East and has its source about 150 miles from Tnpuguen, where the first exploration was made by me, and where the only diggings have been established. The medium breadth of the Yttruary is about thirty feet ; its depth is insignificant, excepting in a few places where there are deep holes. Its banks are generally high, and seldom admit of being overflowed. The particular spots where the river could spread are easily known, though generally covered with forest. These are the alluvions form by the river, where without doubt, gold must be found just as in the river ; still I am not aware of any one having tried to make a similar discovery. The bed of the river is formed of loose stones, and ofien contains large rocks. Though I have diligently searched for it, I have seen but little or no sand. Whenever I have washed souie of the sandy earth of the river, I have found particles of gold. To meet with large pieces it is necessary to dig out the bed of the river, until a stratum of blue clay is reached, upon which lies the gold deposit. This stratum of clay is met at a depth of from 1 to 3 feet. There are some places so rich that a few hours work a man might obtain twenty dollars Worth of gold, also pieces weighing from twentyfive dols to thirty dollars. These nuggets me iB the neighborhood of Tupuguen F rom what

I have seen, I believe the earnings average from six to ten dollars per day. 1 must here add, that all the small rivers or rapids I have explored contain the same portion of g on have also explored many other places Id. 1 the hills and in the plains, and a most every where have met with the same clay impregnated with gold. The grounds are so thickly covered with quartz as to give it a very peculiar aspect of the country when the sun shines upon them In conclusion I have to say, this beautiful country is by no me ins unhealthy, with such a river as the Orinoco, and such wealth as its soil produces must one day become, eminently prosperous and rich Roads could be constructed with great facility, owing to the dryness of the soil and the, absence of marshes as well as of long ridges of mountains which it would bo difficult to travel. 1 hope I may have explained myself with sufficient clearness I have, endeavored to be true and nothing else. Yours, &c., L. PLASSARD.

Cuidad Bolivar, May 12th, 1853. Dear Sir. þÿ I received your esteemed favor of 28th ultimo, requesting me to state the changes, improvements, or new diggings discoveries that might have occurred at the gold mines of the Yuruary ; I have however but little to add to my report of 2nd July of last year. My opinion regarding the districts in question, so far from changing, has become more deeply rooted, partly owing to subsequent intelligence, and partly because meditation confirmed my earlier impression. So great is the lack of energy amongst the inhabitants of this ouutry, that very few diggers have this year

Sr T , & Ai !/ resorted to the Yuruary. Nevertheless gold has been dug in plenty; and what is still more worthy of notice is their having at lea-t convinced themselves that gold could be obtained without searching for it in the River. The former labor Was the more irksome, aS the men were completely unprovided with t ids. Luckily they have stumbled on some deposits as rich as those they sought underwater. You may probably have seen some of the handsome pieces that have been dug on dry ground. I have no doubt with time, activity and intelligence the day will arrive when Guayana will produce as much gold as the celebrated mines of California and Australia. I must again repeat, that though the pits of the Yuruary will certainly yield an abundant harvest of gold, yet my impression is that these are not the richest spots in the province. According to all the geological phenomenon which I have observed, the most valuable mines will eventually be found more to the southwest. Now, my dear Sir, if to the certainty of finding great quantities of gold in Guayana, we add the number of resources of this beautiful province, it is no idle conjecture to suppose that it must, sooner or later, become the seat of a very numerous population. A REMARKABLE PREDICTION Mr. Caleb Cushing, in his late speech at the public Newburyport, brings reception iven him on his return remarkable to light a home to letter from the Count of Aranda, the Spanish Plenipotentiary who signed the treaty of peace, in 1783, between France, Spain, England and the United States, by which our independence was acknowledged After the conclusion of treaty, the Spanish Ambassador addre-sed turists to the adoption of these varieties of a j a letter to his Sovereign, Charles III,, in which he indulged in reflections npon the future

effects of the great event that had just been accomplished, and in it thus prophecies the destiny of the American Federal Republic, which had been ushered, by the peace he had just concluded, into being: þÿ I have just concluded and þÿsigned, he says, a treaty of pcaco with England, and þÿ this negotiation has left in my mind a painful sentiment We have recognised the independence of the English colonies, and that is to me a subject of grief and dread. France has few possessions in America ; but she ought to have remembered that Spain, her intimate ally, has many which now remain exposed to terrible convulsions. I will not stop to examine the opinion of statesmen, as well countrymen as foreigners who agree with me in estimation of the intrinsic difficulty of preserving our domination in America. Without entering into those considerations, it suffices to content myself with referring to the perils with which we are menaced on the side of the new Power just created in a part of the earth where no other power exists capable of withstanding its progress. This new Federal Republic has come into being a pigmy, so to speak, and in order to attain its independence, has needed the support and the forces of two great Powers France and Spain. The day is at hand when in those regions it will bo a þÿgiant a terrible colossus. Then it will forget the benefits which it has received from us, and will think only of its own aggrandizement. The liberty of conscience, the facility of establishing new

populations in immense territories, and the peculiar advantages held forth by the new Government, will attract thither cultivators and artizans of all nations, since men rush in pursuit of fortune ; and thus in a few years, we shall witness with sorrow the menacing existence of the anticipating colossus. The first stop of this power when it shall have grown to strength, will be to posse-s itself of j the Floridas, in order to command the Gulf of j Mexico. After having thus interposed itself in the way of our commerce with New Spain, j it will aspire to conquer that great Empire, j which it will not be possible to defend against j a formidable Power, established on the same continent, and, what is more, conterminous with it. These apprehensions are well founded, and cannot fail to be realized within a few years, unless indeed, before them revolutions still more disastrous should break forth in our Americas. þÿ Ibid.

The same English papers which shriek at the hare idea of an occupation of the Isthmus of Panama by United States troops in the interest of the commerce of the world, contain the announcement of the annexation of the island of Perun to the dominions of the East India Company. Perim is a small island in the sti aits of Bub-el-Mandeh, commanding the entrance to the Red Sea, and possessing a land-locked harbor capable of sheltering a Heet of ships of the j line. Nearly twenty years have elapsed since the East India Company availed itself of some lawless acts of the Arabs to lay hands on tne fort and sea-port of Aden. At that time it was a miserable place, under the worst climate in the world, with a population of some five or six hundred souls, who starved or made a living by piracy. It is now a thriving place, with a population of over twenty thousand, and has latterly become one of the largest coaling station- for the East India Company's steamers. ; From Aden, looking westward across the str.its. stretches the Souial country and Southern Abyssinia. Behind the Somal desert lies Harar, rich in coffee, spices, ivory, precious m tals, and cloth. With proper securities fbr trade, and some stable authority on the coast, this country could ho developed to a very remarkable commercial activity. To afford such securities, and to establish such authority, was the problem the East India Company set before itself ten or twelve years ago. Several expe-

ditions, with a view to exploration, were uispatched from time to time to tii African coast. Of these t e most notable was that conducted by Lieutenant Bun on, whose woik on Harar has just been published. i he expedition achieved a d .uble purpose : ii indicated where and how the problem could be solved, and it afforded a pretext for armed negotiation with the semi- Arab tribes inhabiting that section of the African coast At Beruera, two years since, a party of English travelers were attacked by the Somali, and a brave young officer killed On this the Company acted. An adequate force was dispatched to the coast, Riid a conference between ibe Airican chiefs and tlie þÿCompany s representatives he.d at Aden. What the arguments used were we, aie left to conjecture ; experience teaches that tue East India Company is not blind to die merits of a judicious mixture of menace and corruption. At any rate, a treaty was made and ratified ; and by that treaty the soveieignty of the island of Perim was ceded to the C inpany, while the British vessels were constituted the supreme police of the nourishing seaport of Berbera on the African coast \\ e imagine, though this is not stated, t hat this police jurisdiction will be found on a pinch to imply actual dominion. It would be idle to argue that, according to | the, law of nations, the English were not justi- ! fied either in seizing Perim, or in assuming control of the waters of Berbera. Nobody, i even in England, pretends to assert tliat they

were. The policy of the British Government is and can only be justified by reference to the j right of the strongest, and on the clear proba- I bility that ultimate good will on How temporary injustice intiicted the despoiled out of the races

We do not, for our part, propose to go out of our way to censure the despoilers. We believe that good will result from their wrong-doing Berbera, under a stable authority, will, no doubt, become one of (lie flourishing seaports of the world j and though the annexation of Perim þÿ which can never he any thing but a naval station, available only for purposes of war þÿ is less directly calculated to be advantageous to the world, we are ready to concede, for the present, that it may be used by the English for the maintenance of peace But, in making these concessions, we desire to draw particular attention once more to the glaring hypocrisy of the English press and a part of the people of England, who revile Walker and his men as pirates for attempting what their own countrymen do eve y year under the þÿQueen f s lag. The spoliation of Oude, the encroachment on Burmah, the ravages in Borneo, the annexation at the Cape, the seizures in Australia, the acquisitions in the China seas þÿ these are events of the past two or three years, and each and all of them are as arrant piracies as any which can be laid to the charge of the most reckless American filibuster. The ruthless subjugation of the Arab races of East Africa þÿ implied in the seizure of their stronghold, and the assertion of police control over their chief sea-port þÿ fitly caps the list, and ought þÿ one would think þÿ to close the mouth of every English enemy to filibusterism for years to come.

Australian Telegraph. þÿ A Select Committee, appointed by the Legislative Council of New South Wales to inquire into the practicability of establishing a telegraphic communication between that colony ami Europe, has made its report. By the evidence it appears that the best way would be to connect Sydney and London by way of Port Essington, Singapore, Rangoon, India, and the Euphrates. There would he no submarine cables between England and the Indian Archaepelago, except across the British Channel arid the Bosphorus. The cost of constructing a telegraph between Sydney and Port Essington þÿ a distance of 1S00 miles þÿ is estimated at £130, 000; and the annual cost including inte st on the outlay, is estimated at .£55,000 per annum.

Carbon. þÿ There are a few facts connected with carbon that merit consideration. Carbonic acid gas, entering the lungs, is a deadly poison ; hut entering the stomach, which lies close under the lungs, and is over-lapped by them, it is a refreshing beverage. Although charcoal, when burnt, gives þÿoil the most poisonous gas, it seems to be very jealous of other gaseous poisons, for if it be powdered and set about in pans where there is a poisonous atmosphere, it will seize hold ot poisonous gases, and, by absorbing, imprison them. Even in a drop of toast-and-water, the charred bread seizes hold of whatever impurities exist in the water; and water passed through beds or charcoal becomes filtered, and made beautifully pure, being compelled to give up to the charcoal whatever is obnoxious. If a piece of meat that has already begun to nitrify he sprinkled with charcoal, it will not only object to the meat petrifying any further, but it will sweeten that which has already undergone putrefaction. Although, in the form of gas, it will poison the blood and cause speedy stupefaction and death if it be powdered, and stitched into a pier of silk, and worn before the mouth as x respirator, it will say to all poisonous gas that come to the mouth with the air, þÿ have taken this post to defend the lungs, and I arrest you on a charge of murderous þÿintention, Such are the various facts connected with carbon ; and they forcibly indicate that those who understand þÿNature s works are likely to receive her best pro-
tection. þÿ The lieasnn Why

(From Harper's Weekly, May 30.) THE ARAB MOHAMMED HABAT. In the Kangaroo, on 14th inst., there sailed from this country an old man whose presence here and whose story are not very fluttering to our national pride. His name is Mohammed Ilabat. He is a nephew of that famous ex-bashaw of Tripoli þÿ Hamet Caramanli þÿ who, in the days of Mediterranean piracies, conspired with our gallant countryman Eaton against his brother, the reigning bashaw. Three hundred and twenty American citizens were then prisoners at Tripoli. To liberate these was þÿEaton object. s Hamet covenanted, in return for þÿEaton aid s and a force of one hundred Americans, not only to set free the American prisoners, but to abolish forever piratical interference with American trade in the Mediterranean. General Eaton started from Egypt in company with Hamet, at the head of an army of some three thousand men, in the month of March, 1805. It had been resolved to proceed by land across the desert. Perhaps army never endured such sufferings before. Water was scarce; the heat was oppressive ; the march long ; the general appointments scant. Many times on the way the Arabs were on the point of giving up and returning home; but the energy and fortitude ofEaton, Hamet, and of his nephew Mohammed Ilabat, kept up their courage. After two þÿmonths journey, they saw Derne, the capital of Tripoli. The of the bashaw þÿ summons, and the characteristic reply þÿ þÿ are known to every one. The word was given to assault. Contrary to expectation, the Arabs fought well; for two days Derne was defended with in-

credible obstinacy. The approach of Commodore þÿBarron s squadron rendering their prospects hopeless, the bashaw at last resolved to surrender. At that moment the peculiar family hatred which is characteristic of Arabs predominated in his mind. He was ready to make a treaty with the Americans, but forgive his brother he would not. The United States Consul, Mr. Lear, in whose mind the safety of the three hundred and twenty American captives was naturally uppermost, gladly embraced an offer of negotiation. He made a new treaty with the bashaw, recognizing him as sovereign of Tripoli, and repudiating the claims of his brother; promising, moreover, to pay a ransom tor the American prisoners, in consideration of the þÿbashaw covenant s to discontinue his piracies in future. That treaty was ratified by Commodore Barron and by the Government of the United States. Poor Hamet Caramanli thus saw himself, in the hour of victory, deprived of the fruits of his enterprise, and considerably worse off than he would have asked his business. He refused to exbeen had he remained in Egypt and scouted the offers of General Eaton ; while this country obtained all it wanted at much less expense than it could have done had the brave Arab refused to participate in the struggle. Those, however, were ingratitude. General Eaton, returning home, was treated with marked neglect and injustice. As for poor Hamet Caramanli, he was glad enough to save his neck from the clutches of his blood-

thirsty brother, and to betake himself to his old home in Egypt. He lived some four years in solitude, bewailing Ins hard fate, and reviling the United States for their ingratitude; then died, leaving ! what a country þÿ!

$ Si © l) 4 Hj (j $ « his family to the care of the pacha, Mohammed Ali. The trust was faithfully discharged. Mohammed Ali took care that the house of Hamet stood in no want during his long lifetime. But when he died, in 1842, the wolf came. No pension was thenceforth paid to the descendants of the injured ex-bashaw, and naturally they starved. In 1856, some Americans resident in Egypt suggested to Mohammed Habat, that, if he made an appeal to the United States Government in person, he might obtain redress. Money was raised for his journey, and he departed. A remembrance of the fate which befell a like appeal from the descendants of Beaumarchais ought to have taught his friends better. He arrived in this country, and laid his case before the Government. Mr. Pierce was at that time regulating the affairs of Kansas; Tripoli had no vote þÿ the petitioner no means of interesting the lobby. Moreover, in truth, though the hardship of the þÿArab s native families of India to establish case was patent, it is not clear that he had a legal claim on the Government of the United States for redress. With the example of British pensions before our eyes, it is well for the United States Government to be chary of establishing precedents of pecuniary indemnities for such wrongs as Mohammed Habat's. His appeal failed, and lie returned to Europe with some aid raised by private subscription. We are inclined to regret that his friends, who must have seen from the outset the hopelessness of an appeal to government or Congress in

his behalf, did not direct their solicita- Your head or mine þÿ! tions rather to the public of this country. With all his faults, the American citizen, individually, is the m ist generous of men; and we doubt not, had a general appeal, based on the facts of the case, been addressed to the public of the United States, it would have obtained the universal approbation of the press and a great measure of success among the public. case shows what may be done with a little energy in a good cause. Hereafter, the friends of persons in the situation of Mohammed Habat will do well to remember that, while the United States Government and Congress have and ought to have no bowels, the American people are uncommonly provided with that excellent commodity, and applications for relief or indemnity should be made to them. a CjIIUSTIANSTLD, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 2 1st JULY, 1S57. By the arrival of the Magdalena at St. Thomas we are placed in possession of European Papers to the 2nd Inst. Dulness in the Political World reigns supreme; and, judging from the contents of the late papers, Editors are at a loss for readable matter. It will be gratifying to the advocates of African Immigration to learn that, since the deputation headed by the Earl of Shaftesbury, waited on Lord Palinerston, the English Government has been far iroin idle in this branch. Another deputation, in reference to this subject, waited on Lord Palinerston of the 24th June. In connection with this subject it will be seen that the Governor of Martinique opened an extraordinary session of the Council General of that Colony on the 4th June, for the special purpose of deliberating upon a question for extending African immigration, submitted by the Minister for the colonies. We hope that our Government will soon take some steps in the matter.

" O," to proposal The this Community, to petition the of our Correspondent, Government to throw open to the public the meetings of the Burgher Council, is one, which, at first sight, might appear very reasonable, but which is nevertheless encompassed with difficulties not easily surmounted. For our part, we should like to see the law carried out as it is; which, since it has been put in force, we have not yet had the pleasure of seeing, before we advise any alterations.
If the proceedings were immediately published after every meeting, all the objects which might be gained by the publicity of the Council's meetings would be attainable.

Inter-Colonial. THE FRENCH ISLANDS. From the Grenada Chronicle 4' Gazette, July 4 The Governor of Martinique, Count de Fitte de Soucy, opened an extraordinary session of the Council General of that c >lony on the 4th of June, for the special purpose of deliberating upon a question for extended African immigration, submitted by the Minister for the Colonies. The following is a translation of His Excellency's speech on the occasion : þÿ "Gentlemen, þÿ Conformably to the commands of his Excellency the Minister of the Marine and Colonies, it has become my duty to convene you in extraordinary session, for the purpose of submitting to your deliberations a question, the importance of which demands your most earnest consideration. "You are aware of the many efforts already made and being made by the Government of the Emperor with the object of supplying to the Antilles the force needed for the development of labour and industry. The results of the measures hitherto pursued with that view have not as yet been fully attained, a d as the necessity continues peremptory and incessant, it becomes necessary to resort to new arrangements. " African immigration seems to present advantages in a way which permits of action upon more enlarged basis. A ship owner has come forward to undertake to furnish you with 10,000 immigrants in five years; but before coming to a decision, or entering into engagement with him, the Minister of the Marine, with a kind feeling of equity, has deemed it proper to submit the proposed terms and conditions of tlio

contract, as well as the consequences which should flow therefrom, to your intelligence, your experience, and the wisdom of your counsels. " The Director of the Interior will place before you all the particulars of this important matter, as also certain questions relating to the detail of the current service, which require your intervention. " Happy, Gentlemen, of a circumstance which brings me amongst you for th : first time, and proud in being surrounded by chiefs of the administration, whose zeal and devotion have, for a series of years in the colony, so well sustained the excellent administration of my predecessor, I come to request your assistance, and frankly and fairly to offer you my co-operation in all things. " We shall understand one another ; for, being alike animated by a desire to promote the good and prosperity of the country, it cannot be otherwise ; and we shall move onwards together by a firm and assured step in that path of improvement and progress which is the aim of the constant solicitude of our Sovereign, whose name I can never proclaim with too great enthusiasm þÿ Vive l'Empereur ! The session of the Council General is opened-"

(From the Illustrated London News.) FRANCE. Count Paul de Kisseleff, the Russian Ambassador, went on Saturday last to St. Cloud, to deliver to the Empress, on the part of his Sovereign, the Grand Cordon of the Order of St. Catherine. The Emperor left Paris on Thursday morning for Chalons and Plombieres. He will remain two days in the former town, in order to inspect the preparations making lor the great camp, and will then leave for Plombicres. The subject of the elections still continues predominant in Paris. At four o'clock 011 Monday afternoon, the voting, which commenced on Sunday morning, terminated throughout France. So far as Paris is concerned, the elections have excited a movement far greater than were generally anticipated. It was not so much lelt on Sunday ; but the whole of Monday, and particularly the early part of it, the people was up and stirring. The right of taking out voting tickets continued up to the moment of closing the ballot-boxes, so that, between the crowds who flocked to take out their bulletins, and those anxious to deposit them, the mairies and the other votingplaces were crowded to the utmost. The results of the Paris elections are as follow: þÿ Of the ten circumscriptions into which Paris is divided Government candidates have been returned in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 7th, 8th, 9th and 10th districts; in the 3rd, 5th, and 6th districts, Cavaignac, Carnot, and Goudchaux (Republican candidates) have been respectively returned. The 3rd district (where Cavaignac was returned) and the 4th and 7th districts (in

both of which Government candidates were returned) have, however, ended without result þÿ the absolute majorities of the whole numbers of registered electors in those places, as required by law, not having been obtained ; and a second election for those circumscriptions will, therefore, take place, commencing on Sunday, July 5. The success of the electoral demonstration in Paris against the Government of Louis Napoleon has far surpassed the most sanguine expectations that the Republicans had allowed themselves to entertain. Two of the Opposition candidates, MM. Carnot and Goudchaux, have been elected by enormous majorities Cavaignac is at the heud of the poll ; and, although his election is not definitive, owing to his not having obtained an absolute majority of the registered electors, there can be no doubt of his being elected at the second trial on Sunduy, July 5. In the fourth circumscription, the rival oppo-ition candidates, E. Olivier and Gamier Pages, obtained between them within 143 votes of the score of the Government candidate, M. Varin. In the seventh, M. Lanquetin, the Government candidate, had but 236 more votes than those given to MM. Darimon and Jules Bastide. In both these latter circumscriptions the bare majority of the Government candidates is insufficient, and there must be new elections. M Gamier Pages has withdrawn in favour of M. E. Oliver; and M. Bastide has also retired in favour of M. Darimon. There is, therefore, a great chance that these candidates of the Sieclc and Pnsse

will be elected on Sunday week. It must be recollected, however, that the Government, relieved now from the anxiety of the general elections, will concentrate all its energies to prevent their return, as well as that of General Cavaignac. Only six Opposition candidates have been definitively elected : þÿ MM. Carnot and Goudchaux, in Paris; Dr. Henoo, at

(f B) Oj (i & A V L s, Lyons; M. Cure, at Bordeaux; M. Brume, at Lille ; and M. Javal, in the Yonne. Out of the 267 elections throughout France, only six will have to be repeated, three in Paris, as stated, and three in the provinces þÿ namely, one in the Maine-et-Loire, one in the Mayenne, and one in the Somme. As a set-off to the six candidates named above, the Opposition has lost the five deputies belonging to it in the last chamber þÿ viz., Count de Montalembert, the Duke d'Uzes, and MM. de Civrac, Charlier, and Desmolles. The Opposition has brought forward 115 candidates in fifty-eight departments, so that it has been defeated in 111 places.

The Emperor of the French has been accustomed to give " warnings" to the newspapers. Ho has now received a warning in his own person. For the first time since the coup d'etat Fiance has given a sign of political vitality. The election, by three of the divisions of Paris, of General CaVaignac, the ancient rival of the Emperor for the Presidency of the Republic, and of Messrs. Goudchaux and Carnot, two of the most eminent members of the Provisional Government of 1848, is the most remarkable event which has occurred in France since Napoleon III. ascended the throne. Much curiosity will be felt throughout Europe to learn if the circumstance will produce any effect on the policy or the position of the Emperor. Will he look upon this victory of the Republicans þÿ lor victory it is, and pregnant with victories to come þÿ as a friendly notice that it is time to relax the rig mr oi his system, and to give the French the small modicum >f crown of the edifice of which ' ie laid the foun- liberty which he solemnly promised as the dations in blood ? Or will he consider it an act of hostility, and so tighten his grip upon the popular throat as to prevent even a cry or a groan for freedom 1 To us outsiders, who watch the evolutions of the great game which the French are playing, it seems that one or other of these results must inevitably follow To restore the stutus quo ant is impossible. With such men in his Corps Legist iti/', Na,>o- 1 on III. must either give the French a greater

degree of libcity or abiid.ot c litt e lileity which they have. The Lm,.ire has cnteied upon a new phase of its existence, i ihe whole world will watch its g:t . Hitherto the Emperor h If it had been his will an nate his Corps Legistatif f good behaviour of its nn . . <1 chosen after his own elect <..i i c ><> be the solo elector as well as de , uutur of France, and to have aboln u ..II other appeals to the people as useless farces or imp rtiuent interferences with his supreme authority and prerogative, there would have been no me strong enough to prevent him Ilis obb juious and admiring army would have approved and aided him ; Paris would have sulkily and reluctantly, and the provinces patiently and stolidly, acquiesced in the decision ; his puppets would have danced on the wires set in motion by his foot ; and his clciks would have drawn their wages and regist red his decrees with the docility befitting the model servants of the model despotism But the Emperor did not choose to do this. He allowed the French a modicum of liberty ; and at the liist favourable opportunity a portion of the me . opolis has taken advantage of the concession to throwin among the Imperial clerks, three men whose names are identified with a dilieiont system, and with the remembrances of the greater liberty so lately enjoyed by the na'ion. The Emperor has exhibited in his remarkable career many proofs of greati s and wisdom. The time seems approaching when he must display these qualities in circumstances

very different from those which have hitherto called them forth, if be would escape many serious dangers He is still the most popular man in France; he is still at the head of an obedient and numerous aimy, whose glories and hopes are intimately connected with the name he bears, and the pretensions which he has set up ; he is still the Elect of millions of the French peasantry ; and in the powerful position of one whose opponents have no claims upon the French people which are not either

ridiculous or obsolete, or both combined. Having allowed the people comparative liberty of election, he can afford to respect the choice which they have made, and to see without terror a minority of Republicans in his mock Legislature. The Chamber may be less slavish than the last : but he has a large majority, and may work the State machine as before, and perhaps more easily, if he be wise enough to relax, in ever so small a degree, the string ncy the system which he established, and which he oas hitherto so unflinchingly maintained. But, difficult as may be the part which the Emperor will have to play, that which the successful Republican candidates will have to play will be moie difficult still. They cannot by the, Constitution, which is their sole title to seats in the Corps Legislatif, exercise their functions until they take the oaths of allegiance to the Emperor. Will they take those oaths? We expect they will, for political oaths among our neighbours are glibly taken and easily broken, or Napoleon III. would not at this moment be Emperor of the French. If they do not take them their election is null, the Emperor triumphs, and the Liberal party is checked and loses its opportunity. If they take them they are the sworn servants of the Empire, within the limits of the Constitution ; and if they attempt to overthrow it, will incur the penalties of treason and of perjury at the hands of a man who is not likely to be merciful towards them. If between them and the Empire there is mortal antago-

nism, they will have much to do before they can imitate the Emperor's example in the coup d'etat, and prevent treason from being treasonable by making it successful. In the meantime, whatever be the groove in which Necessity or Policy may force them to run the Emperor has all the advantage of the position j and, by knowing how to yield, may lay the foundations of his throne far deeper than he could lay them by ultra-despotism. All experience shows that thrones supported by the respect of the people are far more secure than those which depend upon corruption like that of Louis Philippe, or upon force and corruption like that which was inaugarated in 1852, and which has now received its first warning. The French are not naturally a corrupt people. It was t e shameless corruption of Louis Philippe that brong' t him to ruin; and it is the shameess corruption of the jobbers, the parasites, and the knaves who surround the Emperor that has perhaps had a greater effect in profiling the return of Messrs Cavaignac, Goudcliaux, and Carnot, as living protests agiinst it, than any mere preference for a Republican over an Imperial form of government, þÿ

HAYTI. The following remarks on Hayti are so pertinent, that we consider them worthy of being as extensively circulated as our own columns. They are from the pen of Mr. F. W. Che-son. Hayti is a country unfortunately but litt'e knowu in England, and is generally associated with sanguinary revolutions, and scenes of disaffection and blood. But while a retiospect of Haytian history may, to a great extent, justify this idea of the country, as far as the past is concerned, it by no means follows that that idea is applicable to the present state of affairs. On the contrary, we have great reason to believe that, under the firm and enlightened rule of the Emperor Faustin, aided by men of experience and wisdom, Hayti has entered upon an era of peaceful prosperity, during which she will make equal progress in the development of her material resources, and the cultivation of those moral qualities which constitute the chief glory and strength of a nation. Few Englishmen (as far as our observation extends know much either about the geographical position of Hayti, or the character and condition of her people ; and yet the communication between the two countries is direct and frequent, and they are engaged in a large arid lucrative trade with each other, as many Euglish merchants are able to testify. Hayti is second to no country in the world in the fertility of the soil and the excellence of her produce. Her coffee, oocoa, sugar, cotton, and mahogany are world famed ; and we believe that, in the matter

of cotton particularly, she will ultimately be enabled to perform an efficient part in removing the necessity for the almost exclusive use of slave-grown ootton which is now unhappily imposed upon us. But Hayti possesses other claims upon our attention besides those which are derived from the richness of her soil and the value of her natural produots. In the various mechanical arte, especially in those which, like cabinetinaking, require more than ordinary skill, the Haytians greatly excel. The following extract from an article on ' The Industrial Arts of Hayti" written by a young Haytian, M. Dorvelas Dorval, will afford our readers some idea of the mechanical progress which his country has already made : In the plains of tho Artibonite were made formerly some coarse cotton stuffs, known by the name of basalouan, hammock-cloths, girths, for saddles, ropes of the palm-tree, and baskets, and other objects of straw. Embroidery in silk, ootton, and gold thread of different shades, arid the making of artificial flowers and fruits in wax, also occupy the delicate hands of our young city girls. Tanning, although not of the most perfect kind, shoemaking, harncssmaking, hatmukiug, goldsmithing, and ooaohmaking, all afiord products worthy of notice, and employ many excellent workmen. The tailor's art, practised by Haytian as well as foreign workmen, follows the European fashions. But the business in which the improvement is most evident is cabinet making. It is to some skilful German workmen

that we owe the formation of those young and intelligent Haytian operatives, whose Dumber is increasing every year in our towns, and who make beautiful furniture, after the European manner, and in a highly finished style. There is, indeed, no department of mechanics, agriculture, or even the fine art.-, in which the people of Hayti have not afforded a proof of their ability to keep pace with European civilization. A Haytian friend of ours tells an amusing story of a French bishop who was appointed to a diocese in Hayti, and who went out to the country with the idea that ho was going to labour among a people as barbarous as the negro tribes of Western Africa- What was his astonishme t. on landing at Jacmcl, to find himself surrounded by all the evidences a of an advanced civilization, and weloomed by society whose good breeding and polished manners rivalled the social habits of Paris or London. But the bishop would have felt little surprise at what he saw and heard il he had been previously aware of the existence, throughout tho country, of an admirable system of education. It may not bo generally known that, so far bao't as 1815, King Christophe introduced the Lanuasterian system, under the abls supervision of a number of enlightened Eng-

e i 0; II X, X V lj $ , lish masters, whom he obtained from this country. The country is divided into sixty-five parishes, in each of which a public school is maintained by the Stute ; while in Port-au- Piluce, Cape llaytiaii, Aux Cayes, and other important places, college-, -chcois of medicine, and other superior educational institutions exist, lor the benefit ui all classes of the community. Iu the college- t u English language is taught ; the value ot that acquirement being universally appreciated, especially by persons engaged in mercantile pursuits. All the teachers aie natives of the country, and many of them are persons of remarkable ability and attainments. The Emperor manifests a gieat desire to promote the education ot his people, aud no man is more fully conscious ot the importance of the general diffusion of knowledge as a means of increasing the happiness and prosperity of the country, and thereby adding to the stability of the enipbe. Hence His Majesty exerciser a vigilant guardianship over the national schools, aud endeavours, from time to time, to increase their efficiency aud usefulness. Of the literature of Hayti we will, at present say little, although much might be written thereupon. She can boast ol her historians, ouo of whom, Madiou by name, has acquired some celebrity: she can claim u have given birth to novelists and dramatic and satirical writers of no mean ability; while her Moniteur and Commercial Journal þÿ copies of which we have had the pleasure to þÿreceive prove that she dues not with-

hold encouragement from journalism. No country has been more grossly calumniated than llayti, but never were the primary causes of calumny more apparent The United States ol America naturally regard her with an unfriendly eye, because she is a stauaing protest against the system of negro Slavery, and a convincing evidence of the moral aud intellectual equality of the African race. And while we are gratified to know that the French Government and people are disposed to view Hayti with a friendly eye, yet, unfortunately, some of the public writers of Paris have sought to perpetuate those feelings of hostility towards the former slaves ot France, which were excited by the sueces-l'ul efforts they made to east off her galling yoke. As a consequence of the state of public opinion in America we find the pro slavery party making insidious attempts to obtain such a looting in the hitherto ill-governed atid disorganized republican State of St. Domingo, as will enable them the more effectually to a; tack the independence of Hay t i, which is by far the wealthiest aud most powerful section of the island. But we arc glad to be able to state that General Santana, the President of the Dominican Republic, who, there is grave reason to believe, bad availed himself of his elevated pusition to promote the intrigues of American agents, lias been removed from uffi e amid general expressions of satisfaca pat rim b tion. His simr «or is M. Ruenaveutura Baez, - 0 banished on his elevation ,e Presidentship,

says the Jt laugurated by public rej continues the same ji i v to the residences ot t ,. 'resident, General Reglaun , ajn, England, and F ranee, whe ( c '-iks w« re delivered in celebration of this p ->p tious event." We earnestly w ish that the Journal des Debats exhibited as intelligent an acquaintance with the state of Hayti as it does with that of St. Domingo. But the reverse is the fact; and to such extent has it misrepresented the condition of the former country that the Baron Damier, the Haytian Minister at this Court, felt himself called upon to administer a dignified rebuke to the unfair statements of the French journalist. In his reply ho made the following pertinent remarks : " I beg you and the whole world to believe me when I declare that the condition of Hayti is such as to command respect. She is a State duly organized, and not only progre-siDg, but strenuously and unremittingly exerting herself to attain the height of civilization already reached by the oth r n i' ions of the universe. Her government is an enlightened one. Every unprejudiced and candid foreigner who visits our oountiy is delighted to render it justice, and to acknowledge that the chief to whom it has confided its destinies, my august Sovereign, the Emperor Faustin I., is fully competent to fulfil his mission ; that he has effected wonders for the

amelioration and prosperity of the country, and that he has nothing more atheurt than to sati fy to the utmost the aspirations of all who are interested iu tlie future of the black race. Fully impressed with the conviction of our dignity as a nation, and with a sense of the duties im posed upon us, we shall, with the Lie. sing of the Almighty, and in despite of our traducers, attain a position which will constitute the best justification, not for us Haytians alone, but for every man of our race, to whatever country he may belong. Such is my hope." It is a pleasure for us to turn from the Journal des Debats to pay a tribute of justice to another organ of the French press, Le Courier de Havre , which lias done justice no less to the efforts which Hayti is putting forth to raise herself to an equality with other civilized nations, than to the importance of her geographical position, and the desirability of maintaining her independent existence. The following extract from this article cannot fail to be interesting : " The two allied nations, especially France, ought, for reasons just given by us, to sympathise with that empire and its government and to watch over the preservation of its political existence as a free, sovereign, and independent State. It is r< miirkable to observe the great facility with which European ideas are penetrating into the young and stirring society of that island, which has been laughed at, because people did not understand the unheard-of efforts

made by its inhabitants to constitute themselves into a State. Every day a uew reform is going on : and as the example of France is, to be sure, the best to imitate, ber constitution is being introduced more and more thoroughly into the customs of tiic couutry, and our civil and governmental manners are becoming those ol the Haytians The disposition of that people to imitate FraDce has been laughed at. Ought the coloured population of that island to extemporise a manner of living utterly diffeieut fr- tii that which is rendered unavoidable by the cut it with civilization ? To proscribe imitation n this case would be the same as to return to barbarity. The slanderers of Hayti did in . stand that; they have been witty grata s and without reason ; they did not see that it would have been honourable iu them to n rage these generous efforts, instead of true i abusing former slaves, the heriocal pioi.eeis of progress, who became independent by their valour, and were left to themselves to create a nationality. The man who, better than all his predecessors, understood the future of his country, he who felt in himself the force and energy necessary to overwhelm anarchy and to found a strong and stable government, is the Emperor Faustiu, I. In spite of rebelliou and treuson he goes straight on his way, without caring for obstacles, which he ovei throws in order to arrive at his end þÿ the consolidation of the groundwork upon which lie is raising a government edifice which is to assure the destiuy of his people."

We cannot but deplore as a calamity the continued disunion subsisting between Hayti and St. Domingo. Tho fact simply is, that the island ought not to be ruled by two distinct governments. Imagine the feuds, the jealousies, and probably even the wars, which would arise if England were divided iuto two separate principalities, each maintaining a different form of government, and each pursuing a policy peculiar to itself? Yet such is the actual state of affairs in the island of St. Domingo at the present time ; while an additional misfortune is, that the isolation of the Dominican Republic from its more important neighbour, has enabled foreign intrigue to aim successive bl ws at the independence of the whole cnuntiy. The old adage, "union is strength," is a very hackneyed expression, but, in the case of Hayti i' becomes peculiarly applicable ; and, until it is < aliz d, we shall not think that negro capacity for selfgovernment will have had a fair trial. T e union of the two States under on.- government would form a far more effectual guaiantee of the permanent independence of the entire nation, and of the triumphant discomfiture of foreign marplots, than any engagements into which France and England might enter, or any display of naval power which they might make in the Gulf ot Mexico or the Caribbean Sea." Production of Oil, Candles, and Spirit from the Earth.þÿ Mr. Stephen White, of Liverpool the well-known patentee of the hydrocarbon gas, or gas from water, has succeed ed in obtaining very singular and valuable products, applicable to a variety of useful purp ses, from a peculiar oil which flows spontaneously from the earth into wells at Rangoon, in the Barman Empire. These wells are in great number, and are about 150 feet deep The oil flows into them continuously, and ie drawn up by the Burmese in iron pots, aud collect, d. The annual produce of these springs of oil is upwards of 90,000 gallons : it is used by the natives for cooking, torchlights, aud other domestic pu poses. Air. White has patented his invention. lie subjects the crude oil to distillat on in a novel atid ingeniouslyarranged series of stills, working together, the one into the other, which produces at the same time three distinct substances þÿ viz., parafine, perfectly solid ; an nil, and a spirit The parafine is obtained in very large quantities, and. when purified, is beautifully white and transparent. When made into candles it burns with a brilliani-y unequalled by any other substance. The oil, when subjected tothe purifying process, is obtained almost colourless and transparent, is extremely valuable for lubricating the lino machinery of the cotton, silk, linen, and woollen manufacturer ; and lias better lubricating properties than the finest sperm oil þÿ which of late years has become scarce and much adulte-

rated with inferior oils. þÿ J lie patent oil affords a clear and powerful light when burned in a lamp; and li s tho singular property of preserving metals from the corrosive influence of tho atmosphere, or salt water, &c. ; when applied to the copper coating of ships, the preservative effect is very striking. From the Jamaica Despatch.) The Supply of Labour. There are several facts respecting our labourers, the examination of which may help to elucidate the labour qu« stion ; some of which are remarkable enough. In certain districts you find masses of labourers brought from their homes twenty or thirty miles off in search of labour, attracted only by regularly paid wages at a shilling or fifteen pence a day, and contented, in order to get that, to live huddled promiscuously in out houses, without the comforts of a home to fix them to the place. lu other localities resident labourers abound, steeped in poverty, but determined against working continuously ; or, when they do work, they refuse to do so beyond five or six hours a day. And, there is the third case, where the planter has no difficulty in getting all the labour that he wants, so long as he has money to pay for it liberally and regularly. There is further this remarkable fact ; although the labouring class necessarily constitutes the bulk of the population of a country like this, recently emancipated from slavery, yet that population now hardly make one fifth of the exportable products of sugar and coffee, which they made fifty years ago. The cultivation of the majority of the plantations on which they then worked has been abandoned, and the owners or lessees of those in cultivation cannot get labour to carry them on. Whence this anomaly? It is but a few of our poorer labourers who have risen to the position of independent agriculturists ; and we see no

extra productions of their labour, either in our home markets or in our tables of exports. The irresistible conclusion, therefore is, that desultory indolent habits, arising from a low domestic condition, aggravated by a long continuance of low prices and consequently low wages, have greatly impaired the industrial efficiency of our people. But it is not universal, nor is it at all a peculiarity of the negro. Mr. Henry Mayhew, in his statistics of crime and its causes in England, imputes the same incorrigible habits of idleness, and preference of desultory and vagrant life to regular industry, which is a characteristic of a large proportion of the criminal population, to the want of a proper domestic condition, and moral and industrial training in infancy and youth. An utter indifference to the rewards of industry, and to the comforts of home is ultimately induced; and the character is seldom reformed. Such 1 fear is the condition of a large portion of our population, and from the same causes. These facts throw light on the elements of our labour question, and point out as the course to he taken to secure a supply, the reform of our social condition. Importation has hitherto been too exclusively regarded as the remedy þÿ its operation is considered to he immediate þÿ but aftev expending upon it nearly half a million, and rendering its existence almost intolerable by excessive taxation, the evil remains where it was. Besides, our immigration schemes have entailed upon the country the evil

of mixed races, languages, and religions, heathen, Mahommedan and Christian, with a large diffusion of new forms of vice and immorality ; while we have neither religious nor educational means in operation to check or to modify these great evils.

$ T? C) 1 Q) 0 $ A \r r; $ « What kind of men and wonrmn do the neglected children of European families become? Just as idle and worthless as the neglected of negro families. What would you xpect ot a European woman with half-a-dozen of illegitimate childtheir suppr ren, who had no certain dependence for , or means for their educational or religious ttaining, obliged to toil out of doors for her own and her þÿyoungsters bread, and to leave them alone to the innumerable chance-influences of evil, that abound everywhere in country life in this island. Such in Europe is a comparatively rare domestic condition, while here the contrary of it is the exception. The Rectors of several parishes have informed me that not less than 75 per cent, of their baptisms are of illegitimate children. The Legislature may think that moral evils are not within its province ; but it ought to be remembered that t1 se are the roots of the worst evils in the body po.itic. Accordingly, the Governments of Europe, and in a remarkable degree the Governmeat of England, and many of the most eminent of her nobility and gei.try, are now devoting their attention to social | and educational questions as the lead- ! ing subjects cf their attention. Would that wv had amongst us indication of a like spirit. We have hardly any efficient schools for the humbler classes ; we have no industrial philanthropic, or reformatory institutions whatever. A smattering of reading and writing communicated by a few very poorly paid and generally incompetent teachers,

is all that our people have, and to a great proportion even that is not available ; the education of the mind and the sentiments has been impossible with such an agency; and as to religious training we know that the parish clergy generally do not even profess to give it to lli 'ir people. The m.i-ses therefore are without religious instruction suited tp their capacities. We require other þÿ than the weekly half hour in the pulpit we need daily labours in district meetii gs and domiciliary visitings. Ecclesiastical ornaments from Universities 0 ght not to eat up the little which this overburdened country can afford for the substantial religious training of the population of our parish) s. 1 concliid , 'lieu, that þÿthi aversion to continuous labour so characteristic of our people, is in a great measure to be traced to the c.ois -s which have created in England a cl .ss with pr, cisi lv similar characteristics; with ilos exception in our favor, that those crimes of deeper live, the fruits of utter despair caused by destitution of warmth and food, do not, and cannot so greatly prevail amongst us. When the Labour question comes to he considered again by our Legislature, 1 trust that some more comprehensive view than a mere supply by importations may have attention. The evils of a neglected condition of the population now press heavily upon us þÿ it has almost choked native industry. But, it is never too late to attempt amendment ; and I trust that our great sufferings and adversities, incontestibly en-

gendered by such a condition of the people, may induce those at the head of our affair, henceforth to make the social condition of the country the main object of their attention. For assuredly, while ignorance and a low social condition of the labouring classes is the life of a slave þÿcountry prosperity s ; the very contrary is the law and the condition on which the prosperity of free countries depends. N bidding farewell to this island, where I have lived for upwards often years, and enjoyed my best portion of earthly blessings, I cannot find words adequate to express my feelings of gratitude for the great benevolence and kindness I have constantly met with in this community at large and more especially among the members of the Congregations whose Pastor I have been for a length of time. The unparalleh d sympathy which has been shown Xo me from all sides in the hour of my leaving the island has made a deep impression upon my mind. I have nothing my dear friends to offer in return for all your kindness towards me and my family, but a sincere prayer, that God Almighty may be graciously pleased to each and to bestow upon prosper this island, and all of its inhabitants all the spiritual blessings of a true christian life. As for myself, my dear friends, I only beg you to remember, that I leave your beautilul island with the humble prayer, that God in Heaven will iorgive and that you will forget my faults. ALEX.
