PAR.MA. Letters f om Parma bring some very pleasing news. The regular troops, and the volunteers from that Duchy, after serving under Charles Albert during the national wars in Lombardy of 1848 9, received front that King the distinction of gold or silver medals, hut, soon after the restoration of the Ducal Government, were forbidden to wear those honourable insignia, won by them upon the field of battle. The present Ministers of the remonstrances Duchess Regent, of M. yielding to the friendly Minister to the Courts Boncorripagni, Sardinian of Tuscany, Modena and Parma, have coma to the resolution to allow their soldiers full permission to wear all such orders and medals as they had received Government which the Parmese in those wars, an act by not only give evidence of their sense of justice, hut also of their tendencies towards a Piedmontese, t. e., national Italian policy.

FRANCE. PARIS, Thursday, May 28, 6 p.m. The Republican party, it appears, bus decided on putting forth a certain number of candidates at the approaching elections in Paris. These candidates belong to what used to be called the Bluet or moderate Republicans, and

are General Cavaignac, M.M. Havin, Goudchaux, Marie, Bethmont, Lasteyrie, Carnot, Gervais (de Caen), and Gamier Pages, several of whom were members of the Provisional Government in 1848 M. Gamier Pages will also be proposed at Valenciennes and Douay, M. Jules Favre and Dr. Henin at Lyons, and M Maillard, who, I believe, was formerly secretary to M. Ledru Rollin, in the department of the Correze. It is not said whether all or any will, in case of election, take the oath of allegiance to the Emperor. It will be curious to observe the effect produced on tho Parisian population when such names are put before it after so long a period of repose. Of the success of the movement it would be hazardous to say anything, as the Government will probably do their best to keep the doors of the Legislative Chamber shut in the face of men like Cavi ignac. Carnot, and Lasteyrie. As yet no animation, no interest in the elections is visible, and unlesssuch a stimulus as this prevail the apathy promises to remain the same to the end. Where there is no uncertainty as to the result people do not think it worth while to break the tranquillity of their every-day existence. Under any circumstance, I doubt whether there will be more than a score of new members in the next Chamber. Five or six may be promo ed to other posts, placed in the half-way stage of the Council of State, or flung up into the fnradiso of the Senate. As many more may be prevented by business or ill-health from returning to the Chamber. About th same

number of incapables þÿ ror or þÿcountry regular " chips in porridge" þÿ men u eless to Empeof whom even the Emperor himself is tried, may be flung aside. A few may get in on the " Opposition interest" without any positive interference on the part of the authorities. I should be surprised if the changes were more, but it is not improbable that more opposition will be manifested in the next Chamber than in the present ; I believe that there are several Government measures which it would not vote were it not on the eve of dissolution. A reocnt article in the London 1 Times' presents tho following views, regarding the decline of Liberty aud Population in Fiance : þÿ France is very poweiful, much richer than she was ; she has a capital which is tho resort of the world, aud a court which yields iu magnificence to none. But of late years, »nd especially since the establishment of the empire, there h is been a strange dejection among the educated classes, and all those who thi .k or profess to think on political subjects. Railways, gold coinage, increase of trade and increase of revenue, have failed to restore cheerfulness to a large class of Frenohmen. Amid the least of prosperity they have always seemed to seo a sword suspended over the country While all Euro e lias been soundiug the praises of France, beeu unsatisfied. The De Profuudis' of the ' France .itself has old political world and the old literary world has mingled with the official Te Deurn of the Imperial þÿretainers. All this was to be expected. In France the liberty which was battled for during 60 years is extinct þÿ certainly for a long timo, perhaps for ever. Can we wonder, then, that the eminent men who gained fame and position amid tliu contests of free political life should in their old age look with anger on the destruction of all they had founded, aud anticipate only decay for the country which has betrayed it-elf and them ! The prevalent feeling which has resulted from these auguiies of ill has been deepened by the publication of the last census. The increase of

population duiing the five years (tiding lt-5t> was only 25 1,003 souls, while the census of li>46 gave an increase of 1,170 003. Now, as the Frenchman is not an emigrant, rarely quitting his oountry to cultivate tho wildernesses of the New World or the Antipodes, this almost, imdiscouraging sign. Not more than 10, 00 French perceptible increase of population is 1 certainly a emigrate yearly ; it follows, there-tore, that the stationary character which population seems now to have assumed must result from some deficiency in prolifio power, tho consequeuoe of deterioration of race or material obstacles which society should remove. There does, indeed, seem to have been lately a rapid diminution iu the rate of increase, until in the present day the increase has almost vanished. But for more than halt a century the French have not been a prolific people In 1720 the population numbered 26/03, COO ; that is, it was almost equal to the population of the British Islands at the present day. At that time Great Britain hardly contained more than 10,0 10,000 souls, while Ireland, with some 4,00 ,003 more, was rather a burden than a support But now things have indeed alteied. The British people have increased and multiplii d and replenished the earth in a manner beyond example. If we take Great Britain alone, we find that the population has considerably more than doubled since the French Revolution, while that of France has scarcely increased more than 35 per cent. Notwithstanding Irish famines and
Engligh strikes, cholera and short harvests, the number of children born has been continually in enormous excess over the deaths But in Franoe

TN. $ ft ft (1 A V k I S . we find that every natural or political calamity checks the increase in a marked manner. In 1847 the excess of births over deaths fell from 23 000, to 62,00 J on account of the scarcity, aud this small excess was again diminished to 13,000 by the cholera of 184y. Things grew worse after 1851. under the double of scarcity and war, till in 1854 and 1855 the deaths for the first time exceeded the births. In consequence of the approaching departure of your reverence and family, to the mothercountry, for ti e purpose of regaining your health, much impaired from the fulfilling of your arduous official duties: we the undersigned members of the Lutheran congregations of the island of St. Croix, in perfect conviction o''your personal merits, are impelled to acknowledge the ardent z al wherewith you have executed the duties of your sacred calling ; as also, to express our gratitude for your untiring exertions for the church and the Christian Communities during the time yon have officiated as a clergyman iu this island. Your active duties were not, however, solely confined to the Lutheran congregations here, but also extended to those of the islands of St. Thomas and of St. Johns when these were without a pastor. We would be ungratefull did we not confess these your merits, as aforesaid, as also, that, as a worthy father of a family, you have always shown a bright example, worthy of all imitation by the congregations respectively, in that the poor and needy ever found in you, a parental benefactor, dispensing with a beneficent hand your charitable gifts in all quietude, devoid of ostentation, and thus effecting much good in secret. As the debilitated state of yottr health renders a voyage to t'ie mother-country imperatively necessary, we beg leave to offer our heartfelt wishes for the welfare, and prosperity of your-

self and family during the approaching voyage, as also in the mother country, and it has been our most fervent wish of soon seeing you again within our cir le, that with renewed vigour and energy you might continue to officiate as a religious teacher in this islan 1, but have learned very lately that another prison has been appointed or nominat d in your place, we can but express our fervent wish and hope that you may obtain in the mother country another appointment adequate to your nurit as afore stated. St. Croix the 19th June 1857. We remain Reverend Sir, your most obedient humble servants, (Signed by 72 members of the Congregation.)

After a while the Government at Washington thought fit to interpret this Treaty as being tantamount to an abandonment on the part of Great Britain of all actual territorial possession in Central America, and especially of the islands situate in the Bay of Honduras, as well as in the light of an abdication of the Protectorate, which had for nearly a century been exercised by Great Britain in favour of the Kingdom of Mosquito. England resisted this interpretation as being not only inconsistent with the absolute understanding of the respective Miuisters at the tiure of the negotiation of the Treaty, but as being wholly foreign to the object with which the Treaty had been negotiated. The usual amount of American gasconade followed, as well in as out ot Congress, and England was threatened, if not wi;b positive annihilation, at least with certain undefined injuries, which appeared to have been better understood at the White House than in Downing Street. The result of all this vapouring, however, was a new Treaty þÿ arranged, negotiat< d, and settled by Mr. Dallas, the American Mi nister to the Court of St. James, and Loia Clarendon, at the Foreign Office. By this new Treaty England yielded in several respects to the demands of the American Government. She consented to give up the Bay Islands to the State of Honduras, merely stipulating that they should preserve their own independ< uce, and be permitted to regulate their own municipal affairs.

She abandoned, as well directly as indii ec-tly, all control over Grey Town, situate at the mouth of the river San Juan, stipula ing in like manner for the neutrality of the port, and its right of self-government. On Saturday the 25th, being the commencement of the Hurricane Season, there will be a general suspension of business and Divine Service will be held in most of the Churches of the Island.

Mutiny of the Indian Army. Our readers will probably recollect that our last advices stated that a troop of the 3J Cavalry at Meerut being ordered on parade to load and Are with the cartridges supplied by the Government, under distinct assurance that no such material had been used in their manufacture as the men seemed to suspect, only five men out of 90 obeyed. The 85 men who refused were at once ordered to their lines, and a court-martial being assembled to try them resulted in their being severally sentenced to a term of imprisonment varying from five to ten years. On Saturday, the 9th inst., a brigade parade was assembled at the station, and the prisoners were ironed on the parade ground in presence of the troops, and marohed off to the gaol. No suspicion seems to have been excited for one moment that a rescue would be attempted, but towards the evening of Sunday, the 10th, while Meerut was wearing the quiet, dull aspect of an Indian station on the Sabbath day, a sudden and furious rise was made by the rogiment, in which, by evident preconcertion, they were joined by the bazaar and townspeople, and by the two native infantry regiments þÿ the 11th and 20th, also cantoned in the place. They at once liberated their comrades in the gaol, and 1,200 other prisoners, and now commenced their bloody work. Meerut is one of the largest stations in India, and before the European part of the force, consisting of Her þÿMajesty 6th s Dragoon Guards, the 60th Rifles, and the Artillery could be assembled half the

station was in flames, and the terrified women and children of our soldiers were in the bands of the savage and Iufuriute orew, who murdered them under oircumstances of unheard-of barbarity. Each officer, as be rushed from his bungalow, to call back the men to their allegiance, was shot down, and ere the European foroe coold reach the lines the bloody work was pretty well completed. At the second volley of the 60th Rifles the mutineers and the whole crew ran, and were followed some milos out of Meerut by the Dragoons, who sabred a considerable number; but by some lamentable oversight the pursuit was now discontinued, and to this we owe a repetition of the dreadful tragedy at Delhi which had just been enacted at Meerut. The mutineers reached that city early on Monday morning, and were immediately joined by the three naiive regiments stationed there þÿ the 38th, the 54th, and the 74th Native Infantry, and by the Artillery, who seem, however, to have done so most unwillingly. During the Monday all the Europeans of the plaoe, except a few ladies and gentlemen who rode for their lives to neighbouring stations, seem to have been butchered ; but, as the place remains in the bands of the mutineers, we may bope that others, of whose fate we have no certain news, have also escaped. The powder magazine feel into their bands, but a gallant young hero, Lieutenant G. D. Willoughby, of the Artillery, is said to have blown up the other magazines, himself perishing with them. The mutineers at once set up a king in the

person of the son of the late Mogul Emperor, and we have no certain news of what has transpired since. The most active measures are of course being taken to suppress this revolt, and it is satisfactory to know from latest intelligence that the garrison at Agra and of the neighbouring stations rsmain stanch. The Commander-in-Cliief is moving down from Uraballa with a strong European foroe, while a oordon of troops of the Gwalior, Bhurtpore, and Putteeallah contingents is being drawn round Delhi to prevent the escape of the mutineers, who will doubtless meet with a speedy and righteous retribution. The conduct of some of the native regiments stands out in most pleasing contrast with that of these scoundrels. Nowhere in India does finer material for an army exist than in Bengal, and it has been the vicious system of pampering and coaxing alone that has led to these lamentab'e issues. An outbreak has also occurred at Ferozepore, but we are ignorant as yet of the particulars. It had, however, been suppressed. Seven companies of the 34th Regiment Native Infantry were disbanded at Barrackpore on the 7th instant. It will doubtless be remembered that it was a sepoy of this regiment who having armed himself with a loaded musket on the 29th of Maroh advanced upon the parade-ground in front of his lines, ana having called upon the mon to mutiny attacked and wounded Lieutenant and Adjutant Baugh and the Sergeant-Major of

£ T ©IOC & D 9« his regiment. The man was tried, condemned, and hung ; and the Jemadar, who was in command of the quarter guard on the occasion, and forbade any of the guard going to the rescue of the adjutant, paid the penalty of his crime also, by the same ignominous death. During the hand to hand conflict that took place hundreds of sepoys in undress and others in uniform looked passively on, while some took part in the struggle, and attacked the officers with the buttends of their muskets. It was not found possible to identify these men, and the Governor in Council determined to disband the whole regiment, with the exception of the three companies who were not present at the station. The order was carried out as above stated on the 7th inst,., the men maintaining the most mutinous and insolent behaviour on the occasion. It is generally felt that these measures are not sharp enough, and that to crush the disaffection which has shown itself very severe remedies must be resorted to. Thus in the short space of ore month have the following regiments disappeared from the ranks of the Bengal army, either by disbandment or by having openly arrayed themselves against the Government. Mutinied at Meerut. The 3 1 Regiment of Light Cavalry. The lltli Regiment of Native Infantry The 20th Regiment of Native Infantry. The Sappers and Miners. Mutinied at Delhi. The 30th Regiment of Native Infantry. The 54th Regiment of Native Infantry. The 74th Regiment of Native Infantry. A Native Battery of Artillery.

Disbanded at Barrackpore. The 19th Regiment of Native Infantry. The 34th Regiment of Native Infantry (7 companies). These regiments represent a force of nearly 8,000 men. If wo have painful proof that disaffection and hatred of our rule arc widely spread in some quarters, we are not without evidence that in others a loyal and intense abhorrence is felt of the treasonable and murderous outbreaks we have recorded Toe youug Maharajah Smdia of Gwalior no sooner heard of the rising at Delhi than be hastened, with every expression of friendship, to place the whole of his contingent at tbo i disposal of the Lieutenant-Governor of Agra. I As a c unpliment to the Prince, the services of his þÿHighness B s ody Guard, consisting ol horse artillery and cavalry, with a detail of infantry, were accepted, the political agent and the brigadier comm .tiding the couliugent having previously inspected them on parade at the express solicitation of (lie P iece. The men of this force are a ve > soldi r ike body of fellows. They are of the same ca-te as the Maharajah, many of them being members of bis family ; and tbeir assist mice, if required, will be loyally given. It is said further that the King of Delhi sent a deputation of the revolted cavalry to the Rajah of Jhind, asking his assistance against the English. Tiie Rajah was on the parade-ground with bis troops at the time, aud immediately ordered bis j soldiers to cut down every man of the messengers. The Rajah Bhurtpore of came forward

also at once with the offer of his regiment, and there is no reason whatever to doubt the perfect j good faith with which these men have acted. The Rajah of Putteeallah lias intercepted and sent to the commissioner of his district many i seditious letters which had found their way into his territories; and so far as we can yet see the districts of the North-West neither desired nor were prepared for the success of the mutiueers at j Delhi, but hold their bloody outrages iu detestation. Perhaps one of the strongest proofs we could have that the disaffection is confined to the ranks of the pampered traitors who have been allowed so long to wear the uniform of British soldiers is to be found in the fact that the very prisoners who were liberated at Meerut have reported themselves to the various police thanadars of their districts, stating their willingness at once | to return to gaol when the Sirkar calls for them. Many have already given themselves up, and it is supposed that not lees than 75 per cent of the whole would yield themselves if called upon j to do so. The fact is the Bongal army is the sole focus j of the mutiny, and its state is a disgrace to the | administration of that Presidency. Over and | over again has the inevitable issue been urged j upon the Government, and we are to-day in the crisis of its eventuation

The first measure called for in our circumstances is an immediate and considerable accession to the strength of our European army in India. A dozen or 20 regiments should at once be despatched from England, aud part, if possible, by the overland route. The second measure should be the immediate appointment of a commission to inquire into the state of the Bengal army. This commission should be composed of officers from the other presidencies and from the þÿQueen s army. The whole Bengal force is demoralized, and it is probable that two-thirds of its senior officers should bo invalided as incompetent, through long training in a vicious system, to enforce discipline. The Bombay and the Madras armies, perfectly free from all suspicion of mutinous feeling, aud in a high state of discipline, are a standing reproach to the Bengal army, and are the sheet-anchor of the Government at the present moment. The opportune return of our European forces from the Gulf enabled us to despatch without landing Her þÿMajesty 64th s and 78th Regiments to Calcutta some days ago, and the troop of Madras Horse Artillery, which was waiting here for transports to convey it to Madras. This force left Bombay a week ago by the steamers Assaye and Queen Victoria, and the transports Raby Castle, Avalanche, and Kingstown. In addition to these troops the 1st Fusil eers bavo been despatched up the Indus, so that the good conduct of our native army and the perfect confidence we have in its discipline and loyalty have

enabled us to despatch a force of 4,000 Europeans to the Bengal side in the last ten days. Madras also is readily furnishing its contingent, and within a month the European army of Bengal will be strengthened by an increase of 10,000 or 12,000 men from the other presidencies. þÿ Bombay Times.

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 2Stii JULY, 1857. We have been informed, that the Burgher Council of this Island has disposed of 360 muskets of the late militia to the Republic of St. Domingo. We are glad to find, that through the means of this sale, the Landtreasury will be enabled to defray the expenses of some very necessary public works. The Court House oi this town, being almost in f dilapidated state, will, we trust, at once be put under repairs. It is disgraceful to our community that our few public buildings are so dilapidated as to be recognized by their dilapidation Our Government House, for instance, is a standing remonstrance against the present Rystem of total forgetfulness of the interest and prosperity of the Island.

We must apologize to our readers for the insertion of the proceedings of so many meetings of the Burgher Council in today s issue. We are led to do so in order that the proceedings may, in future, be inserted in proper time.

From the London Times, June 29. To those who have been in the habit not ; þÿ unnaturally conceived þÿ of regarding tbo Slave Trade question as one fraught with interminable embarrassment, we beg to offer a succinct state- , ment of facts. Attention must first be given to the distinction between the traffic in Slaves and Slavery itself. Against the lattor, as an institution, enough can certainly be said, but with this at present we are not concerned. The practice under the ban of universal law is the Slave Trade þÿ that nefarious aud inhuman commerce by which þÿGod creatures, s being first captured on their native soil, are carried through successive scenes of the most frightful misery till they arc landed upon an opposite coast, to be there sold into lifelong servitude with all its abominations. Tor this, at least, no pica of custom or necessity can be sustained. We cannot be told at this point that the practice has a patriarchal sanction, that it has certain advantages, or that it cannot be terminated without certain difficulties. Whatever may be argued on behalf of domestic Slavery or serfdom, nothing, at all events, can be said for that horrible trade which involves at once the worst kind of war and the worst kiud of theft, and which in all its accessories is so thoroughly atrocious that villauies of the most heinous kind are its natural and ordinary incidents. This, and not the domestic institution of Slavery, is what we are now considering þÿ this is what for so long a time, and with such exemplary perseverance, we have been striving to

put down. Now, what is it that stands in our way ? Under what conditions is this trade still maintained, and how has it come to pass that it cannot be absolutely abolished ? The concurrence of European Governments against the practice is universal and entire, and this unanimity has existed for years. The Powers of Christendom, of every degree, have consented to denounce and extinguish this most detestable of trades, and, this common assent having been stipulated, two of the greatest uations of the wor.d have combined to keep the police of the ocean, so that no contrabandist should attempt what all honest merchants have undertaken to forego. In other words, whereas the Governments of Europe have covenanted, shall their colonies, that Slaves lor themselves and not be importc d into their dominions, the export of these unhappy beings from the soil of their birth is stopped as far as possible by a maritime patrol. What further conditions, we ask, could possibly be required destruction ? As far ns any out for for the extinction of undertakings go, traffic marked every market is closed and every communication interrupted ; yet the Slave Trade is not at but end. þÿits proportions have been diminished, an it exists still, and its victims are still to be numbered by thousands. Ostensibly, all Governments are of one mind, and yet the traffic is not abolished. Where, then, is the obstacle, and what can be done which to all appearance is not done already ? As it happens, we cau put out-

finger without any difficulty on the leak from which the vessel is now suffering. There are no Slaves imported into British Colonics. Our own work has been done thoroughly and is beyond impeachment. There are no Slaves imported into the United States. There aro none imported into the French or Danish settlements, and none now, as Brazilians earnestly assure us, into Brazil. The only receptacle for these cargoes of misery is Cuba; the single delinquent Stato is Spain. But Cuba is nominally closed against Slaves as much as St. þÿVincent or s Trinidad, and Spain does not deny that she, as well as Great Britain or France, is committed by treaty to the abolition of the traffic. Ilow the execution of these conditions is evaded has appeared very plainly in the letters of our Madrid correspondent. The Governor of Cuba is an officer the tenure of whose place is usually brief, and always uncertain, while from emoluments admit of enormous increase his connivance at the forbidden importations. The Cubans are ready to buy Slaves, others are found to fetch them from Africa for sale, and, as there is no class of Spaniards whoso sympathies arc very active in tho matter, the planters can lay in their human stock, aud the Cabinet of Madrid finds it more convenient to employ pretexts and excuses than to exert its authority against its own officers and subjects. Spain, in short, has not entered honestly into tho abolition of tho Slave Trade. It could not for very shame

t, o tens ft refuse its concurrence, but it will not be at the pains of executing its engagements against the will of an important colony, aud it would rather carry on a war of despatches with the British Foreign-office than involve itself in trouble at home. We do not say that this policy contains much to excite surprise, but to the interests of others it is prejudicial in the extreme. The Cuban market keeps the whole Slave Trade alive, perpetuates all the introductory horrors of the traffic in Africa itself, and maintains at their full weight the heavy burdens arising from the preventive squadrons. At the same time, our own colonies aro suffering the most grievous injustice, for Cuba is allowed to thrive on their ruin by its own perseverance in evil, and to supply the demands of Europe through the instrumentality of the very machinery forbidden in the adjaeeut islands. If it were not tor Cuba the Slave 'I rade, so tar as wc can see at present, would be at an end. We do not deny that a policy confined to this species repression of alone is likely enough to be defective, aud that something in the way of substitution for the labour intercepted would probably be iudispensable to the complete and the first and immediate object is concerned the permanent success of our efforts. Still, as þÿ far as interruption of the traffic in human flesh, þÿ we should be apparently accomplishing our ends if the importation of Slaves into Cuba could be stopped. Here, then, are the facts of the case in a very

narrow compass. All countries þÿ Spain included þÿ are committed to the abolition of the traffic, but it continues still at a point of Spanish territory where Spanish authorities are not disposed to repress it. If we can repress it at this point we shall be only doing what Spain hcrselt is bound to do, and what, when pressed, she declares her desire to see done. It has been suggested, as our readers are aware, that we should try the effect of a preventive force on the coast of Cuba, as well as on the coast of Africa, and the gunboats, of which we now possess a serviceable flotilla, have been considered a kind ot craft especially adapted to the purposes iu view. The moral effect, too, of such a policy would be material, aud would prove to the Spanish Government that we weic resolved to insist upon our rights and carry out our engagements. Such a resolution, indeed, we owe not only to humanity, in the cause of which we first undertook the struggle, but to our own colonies. þÿ trade þÿ invincible in their operation prevent us The laws ol from discriminating between importations of sugar. We must buy this commodity in the best markets, and consume it without reference to the circumstances of its production ; but we can, at any rate, endeavour to provide that other settlements, equally bound with our own to abstain from the Slave Trade, shall not take advantage of their own had faith, and rise upon the ruin of more honest communities. We do not, however, deny that this policy,

after all, would be a policy of violence alone, at d as such would be liable to failure at the first period of suspension or indifference. Moreover, it is not for the interests of civilization that productive estates should go out of cultivation, or that an article of almost first necessity should fail in the European markets. We should rejoice, therefore, to see the recent suggestion of certain active philanthropists carried into effect, and a legitimate supply of labour established byproper communications between Africa and the West Indies. Be it remembered that there is no humanity in leaving Africa to itself. Many of its tribes, and especially those near the coast, have been brutalized by the prevalence of the very traffic wc have been considering, and even those of the interior, though less debased, are still savages and heathens. The work of instruction and conversion cannot be more effectually prosecuted than through a system which would maintain a constant communication between Africa aud other parts of the world. Africa is rich in races of men who can endure tropical labour, aud it is allowed on all hands that when Slaves were well treated their condition was superior not only to that of their countrymen at home, but to that of the poorer classes in many parts of Europe. Why should not some such result be now established as a general condition of things ? Why should not the engagement of black labour, stripped of the evils of Slavery by the certified existence of freedom, at once restore
our colonies to prosperity and introduce Africa to better days ? If any person should still be

apprehensive about the position of Negroes in the hunds of planters, under what name soever, we commend to his notice as a final argument that this promises to be the only effectual method of abolishing Slavery. Slave labour, and therefore the Slave Trade, may be driven out of the field by labour of a more lawful description, though it has not yet been extirpated by any means we could adopt. Even if the importation of blacks, therefore, into the West Indies be an evil, it is far tho smaller of the two. Better, surely, have a system of engagements under tho immediate eoguizance of a protecting authority than a system which, in spite of all that can be done, leaves the Slave Trade in active vitality, with all the catalogue of atrocities which follow in its train.

He then exposes it for a quarter of an hour to the fire of a common forge. The crusihle is then allowed to cool, and on breaking it the surface ol the lamp-black coating is found covered with numerous brilliant points composed of sulpburet of potassium; inveloping the crystals of alumina obtained, or, in other words, real sapphires or corundum. The size of the crystals is large in prothose portion to the mass . operated obtained by M Gaudin are upon ; about a millemetre (3-lOOtbs of an inch) in diameter, and balfa millemetre in height. SPIRITUALISM AT BOSTON. On the 4th inst., says the correspondent of a daily paper, a Spiritualist session was held at a private house up town, with Hume and Willis, the Cambridge student, for mediums. Some of the editors of the Traveller and Journal, and other gentlemen of the press, were present by invitation. The whole company numbered fourteen. The room in which the party assembled was lighted by gas, and every opportunity was offered for investigation. The usual feats of moving tables and pianos were performed in the most successful manner in full gaslight, with a sharp-eyed, skeptical gentleman under the table, and halt a dozen others closely watching the mediums, whose feet also were held. The table moved was a heavy extension-table

& i Q 1 JR A\ \( ! & about ten feet long, and on it, part of the time, was the added weight of an editor, whose plump condition does credit to the prosperity ot the profession in Boston. One of the leaves of the table was taken out by unseen agency and laid upon the others. A cloth being placed upon the table, a hand, or what to the touch sennnl a hand, was repeatedly thrust up under it. This was grasped by some of the gentlemen present, in whose grasp it melted away. state that the form and leel fingers was perfectly palpable. The hands of the mediums and of all present were at that time on the table in full sight. Mr. Hume held an accordeon in one hand, taking hold of the bottom of the instrument, while his other hand was stretched out away from it. Several tunes were played upon it by invisible agency. One of the editors present inspected it closely ; he saw the bellows some keys moving exactly as if part and the person were playing upon it, while it hung suspended in the air at only a few inches from his eyes. The result, in short, of the session was, that every body present was satisfied that the feats performed were not done by the mediums, and that any theory of solutions which ascribes them to jugglery is simply ridiculous. þÿ Harper's Weekly.

A NEW LINE OF MAMMOTH STEAMERS. A Liverpool paper says that Mr. Clare, Jim., of that place, is prepared to build four iron mail steamers ot 10,000 tons each, that shall average twenty miles per hour, for the sum of .£400,000 each þÿ boats that, in case of war, could be applied to the Government transit of troops, etc. Now, what would be the result of shortening the voyage to Australia to thirty days? In the first instance, England receives £20,- 000,000 sterling in gold annually from that colony ; the interest upon that sum for one month (the time saved in conveyance) would be £1840,000, and the draft to the same amount, having another thirty days to run, would make a total per annum of £1,680,000 interest, which, added to £840,- 000 would yield the sum of £2,400,000. So that, in one year, £800,000 more than the cost of building this splendid ileet of steamers, suitable for war purposes, would be realized merely by the saving of time. Mr. Clare is prepared to have this number of boats ready in twelve months, upon the Government undertaking to pay him such a rate of postage as the expeditious services he would render would entitle him to ; and the colonists would not object to an additional postage that would bring them nearest England by at least half the time now consumed.

A Nkwly Invented Horseshoe. þÿ A patent has recently been granted to a mechanic of Philadelphia for an improvement in the method of fastening horseshoes. The invention consists in the construction of flanges or lips rising from the front and sides of the hoof, against which they are made to bear, separate, and fastened by sliding into a recess in the side of the shoe, and secured by means of a screw, thus entirely dispensing with the use of nails, and avoiding any liability to injury by pricking.

Influence of the Moon on Vegetation. To prove the occult power of the þÿ Empress of the þÿnight over the vegetable world proceed as follows : Take any quantity of common Peas and divide them into four parts, keeping them separate, then on any spot of ground fit for vegetation, when the season approaches for sowing them, sow the contents of tho first parcel in the first or the second day of the new moon ; the second parcel, sow the first or the second day of the second quarter ; the third parcel, sow on the second or third day before the full of the moon and the last on the second or third day before the moon is out. Now the first parcel will blossom most beautifully, hut will not fruit. The second will blossom and bear very little. The third parcel will not only blossom beautifully, but bear fruit in abundance. The fourth will scarcely rise from the ground.

American. From the Boston Post, July 6. NEW YORK, July 5. The weather yesterday was all that could be desired, the rain having ceased on Friday night. There were several riots in this city yesterday. The most severe riot originated in the Bowery, between a mob from the Five Points and a party of the Bowery boys. The fight was continued with great ferocity for an hour. Clubs, stones, bottles, and fire arms were freely used, and the Five Pointers were gradually driven back. Eight persons were killed in the riot, and about thirty wounded, including several policemen. At one period of the riot the rioters had the streets barricaded, defying the policemen, of whom upwards of 100 were present. Three regiments of state troops were order'd out and kept in reserve, but their services were not required, as the riot was finally suppressed by the exertions of the police. In the minor riots two persons were killed, and 20 or 30 badly wounded. In nearly all these disturbances ex-policemen were conspicuous actors With the exception of these riots among the rowdies, the day past off finely. The military and civic displays were brilliant and imposing, and the fireworks in Brooklyn, Williamsburg, and the other suburbs, were of the most gorgeous description. The pyrotechnic display of the city proper was postponed on account of partial damage to the pieces, occasioned by the damp weather of the week. After the close of the military review, Gen Sanford gave a grand collation at his house, at which Governor King and Mayor Wood were
present, both of whom made speeches in response to complimentary toasts.

( From the Boston Post , July 6.) One of the greatest statesmen of the country has fallen ! William L Marcy is no more ! He began his long, brilliant and noble public career as one of a little gallant band which, in the war of 1812, captured the first flag that was taken from our enemy ; and his last great duty was four years of as remarkable administrative service as the annals of our state department can show. In all the varied stations he occupied it is no more than just to say

® i Q) 0 1 that lie fulfilled public expectation ; and while he won the confidence of his political friends, he con aided the respect of his political opponents. His sudden death, at Ballston, N. Y., cannot fail to produce a deep sensation of sorrow throughout our nation þÿ we may say, throughout the civilized world ; for no statesman of the present day was more widely known or more universally respected. He achieved his great reputation and exalted public positions by his innate mental power, purity of character, patriotic instincts, and indomitable industry. Mr. Marcy was born in Sturbridge, Massachusetts, in 1786, and graduated at Brown University in ,808, when he removed to Troy, New York. In this place he studied law and commenced the practice of this profession, lie took a bold part in sustaining the war and was one of the early New York volunteers to rally around the national standard Soon after the close of the war in 1816, he was appointed recorder of the city of þÿTroy and five years later, in 1821, he removed to Albany, which has continued to be his place of reside < e\cr since. This was the date of the cornu.. u M of his brilliant state career, for in 1821 1 appointed adjutant general. Two yen. þÿin v, , i when New York was prosecuting with bo much energy its system of internal improvements, Mr. Marcy was transferred to its finance department. It was at a critical period, and all parties bore willing tributes to eminent administrative talent which lie then exhibited in

the maturing the measures which placed the credit of the Empire state on a firm foundation. In August 1828 Mr. Marcy was appointed, by Governor Pitcher, to the office of judge ot the supreme court, a selection most satisfactory to the bar and to the democratic party. His judicial career justified this partiality, and three years later, when Judge Marcy was elected to the United Mates Senate, he left the bench Steamship Cahawha, from New Orleans, via with the general regrets of the al le and learned legal profession At this time he was the confidential friend of Martin Van Buren þÿ and was in the full maturity of his great intellectual powers. A political opponent þÿ Judge Hammond þÿ pays to Judge Marcy, at this period of his life, a beautiful tribute. þÿ He was a scholar and a good and ripe þÿone þÿ of elevation of mind þÿ of integrity and impartiality as a judge, and a most accomplished and able political writer. Judge Marcy, so far from seeking or intriguing for the office of senator, accepted it with hesitation and reluctance. He. had hardly occupied this post two yenrs, when he was nominated by the democratic party for the office of governor, where he remained six years. In this position Mr. Marcv, by his firmness and ability þÿ by the just weight of a high personal character, and an already largo exp. rience, acquired the almost universal confidence of the people. They saw in him the quality of þÿstatesmanship for lie was no successful wire-puller, who had chaffered his

principles for place þÿ but an honest public servant, who labored intelligently for the common good. It was in 1836, when the pestilential anti-slavery agitation commenced, that Governor Marcy threw against it, in a message, the weight of his official position þÿ uttering the views of a patriot and a statesman. After service as a member of the board of to adjust the claims of our citizens on Mexico, President Polk invited Mr. Marcy into his cabinet as secretary of war. Here he added to a large reputation. To his wisdom and administrative talent is the country largely indebted for the glorious results of the Mexican war. Then his military experience in active service of the 1812 war, and as adjutant general, were turned to noble account; and his state papers are a monument of his comprehension of plan and vigor of execution, We would not pluck a leaf from the laurel wre.iths of our military heroes , yet it was Secretary þÿMercy iron s will that prevented the jealousies and quarrels of some of our generals from jeopardizing, on the fields of Mexico, our national rights and interests. The last pre-eminent service Mr. Marcy rendered we have from time to time chronicled ; we mean his four years administration of the state department in President Pierce's administration. His masti rly state papers will be among the unimperishable records of the country. His sagacity, foresight, accurate observation, sound judgment, untiring industry, and

admirable execution, have commanded the praise and respect of the candid and intelligent of his countrymen. He has added new glories to the American name þÿ and he did it by his quiet way of asking of foreign powers nothing but what was right and of submitting to nothing that was wrong. His vast knowledge of international law þÿ his keen and unerring logic þÿ his quick and grasping comprehension, were exhibited in his official correspondence and other state papers, in a manner that arrested the attention and excited the admiration of all Europe. Thus at a ripe old age has William L. Marcy gone to his rest. A great man has fallen ! One who has sustained, from youth to age, the rights, interests and honor of his country þÿ whose personal integrity of character was universally admitted þÿ who added to a shrewd knowledge of men the ripest and most varied scholarship, and whose native talent and thorough culture always enabled him to rise to the mark of his responsibilities and his duties. Mr. Marcy was an ornament, and a leader of the democratic party. He was of the Jeffersonian school of polities þÿ and since 1812, is been with the great national party in all its fierce struggles. Much has he contributed to the success of the good old cause. But he has been ever an open and honorable partizan þÿ never viiulent towards his opponents. He was one of whom the party was justly proud. Throughout his varied career þÿ in all the exalted and re-ponsible offices he held þÿ amid all the bitterness of party crimination and recri-

þÿmination no one has been so reckless as to breathe an intimation impugning his personal honor and integrity. In Ins manners he was sometimes abrupt ; but, in all his acts, honest. He was a democrat by nature þÿ a sincere believer in the Jeffersonion doctrine of the capacity of the people to govern themselves, and a despiser of all that frippery, tinsel and display employed to give one man a factitious superiority over his brother man. He was quick to discover and acknowledge moral intellectual and patriotic worth in whatever sphere of life they were exhibited, always anxious for their just appreciation by others. The Failure to take Sebastopol A most thankless discussion, and one which involves the reputation of the dead as well as the living, has been opened by one of your contemporaries, who, being evidently misinformed, has stated that Gen. Todtli ben, in answer to a question whether Sebastopol might have been captured if attacked immediately after the battle of the Alma, had replied affirmatively. Now, I may state on the best authority, that Gen. Todtleben, when asked this question during his recent stay in Germany, distinctly replied in the negative ; he maintained that any attack of the Allies from the south side of Sebastopol would have shattered against the broadsides of the vessels anchored in the harbour, leaving alone the fire from Fort Sievcrnayo, or, as the Allies called it, the Star Fort. He, moreover, affirmed that any assault on the north forts, undertaken without the assistance of siege batteries, and without a knowledge of the ground, would not alone have resulted in the repulse of the Allies, but would have been one of the most unjustifiable acts of military folly ever committed. þÿ Corrts ponden of the. From the St. Thomas Times, August 1.) F1RE!! On Wednesday night last (29th ult.) between eight and nine o'clock a terrible fire broke out in one of the large sheds over at the Careening Wharf, better known as Saubot's wharf, but belonging to the Heirs of James Hazzell, junior. At this place, which is situated over at the southern end of the harbor, and has for many, very many years, been favorably used for careening large vessels, storing of important cargoes, and a year or two ago as the Coal Depot for the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company's Ships, and for which latter purpose it is peculiarly well adapted, had erected upon it several substantial wooden sheds or storehouses, well constructed and immensely spacious, which, at one time or other, have as we 6aid served either for the storing of cargo, coal, spars, timber, and other building material, there happening to be of the latter a very large stock in store when the fire commenced. In the most eastern shed the Sugar and Rum, comprising the cargo of the British barque Mary Bibby, from Demerara in distress, and undergoing repairs there for some months, were tored ; this cargo having miraculously escaped the ravages of the flames, has served to mitigate the. horrors of the scene to a remarkable degree, for had the puncheons of Rum, about 18 proof, ignited, they would have ascended in the air with the force of shell or rockets, whilst some of their fragments after bursting might have fallen among the shipping lying near to the shore. Fortunately, we have not to record such calamities while endeavor-

ing to describe others. It is enough when we state that of the four large sheds there erected three were consumed, in each of which there wns either coal, spars, timber, copper, or some other matter connected with a ship-yard ; these articles, we believe, totally belonged to the firm of Messrs. A. Saijbot & Co., who hold a lease of the premises, and mu-t in consequence be terrible sufferers by this conflagration. Without any hazard of making an overestin ate we may venture to place the loss in mova le stock at Thirty Thousand Dollars, for we hip told that as a first item there were 1600 tons of coal, that until now continues a burning mass, and which at the cost of landing here may be set down at $8,000, but at its market value would be nearer $16,000 j the spars are estimated at $5000 þÿ and so we could go on enumerating, and easily arrive at the figure mentioned above. It is only to be hoped that for the good of the parties concerned this laige amount of property may be covered by a policy of insurance. Let us also hope, for the sake of the human heart, that the origin of the fire may prove to have been accidental, for it is admitted that the most heinous, cruel, and diabolical crime that man, acting like a fiend, can conceive or commit is arson For he knoweth only when the brand, which he hath lighted, commences its evil, but can foim no judgment when and where it shall end ; and he thereby lays a train of mischief which in its progress reaches the widow, the orphan, the helpless and blind,

who possibly enjoying the benefits of a home, bear with resignation those other trials of which they suffer, but by his hands they are þÿ houseless and wanderers on the streets if a made more direful calamity docs not attend them, by their falling a prey to the flames. It is for this reason that the incendiary, in a less enlightened age, has been bound to the stake, and made to feel the tortures of that very element with which he had consummated the destruction of others. The rapidity with which the flames had gathered strength made it apparent to all who reached the spot, or those who with telescopes from the hills in town surveyed the catastrophe, that no human exertions could be enough to arrest tneir progress, and that the fire would continue to last as long as it found material to feed upon. It is, however, pleasing to us to aaccrtain that to these conclusions there, are valuable exceptions to be made, and that the eastern slied þÿ the most important one, and containing much value þÿ was rescued through the intrepidity and untiring perseverance of a few who had timely reached the place, and whose temerity allowed them to ascend the

S> þÿT $ B ® t) S «l t (1 «. roof and keep extinguishing the fire as fast as it would seize upon the wood. It is at all times unpleasant to particularize any one individual, where all are exerting themselves, yet we believe we would be omitting our duty were we to refrain from mentioning the name of Mr. John Blackwood, shipsmith, who, when on the roof, approached the fire so near as in some instances to induce him to lift the burning shingles and throw them to the ground ; to his laudible daring, we believe, is mainly attributable the saving of that valuable store. Unfortunately in our community we have no Corporations, no Insurance Companies, no Societies, who assume to themselves the duty of awarding merit, by some substantial token, where merit is due. By our present course we are ourselves the sufferers, for the incentive is lost on future occasions, when it is observed the cold and indifferent manner in which a public receive such d> eds ; were it not so, there are many now in our midst who would possess something wherewith to remember a remarkable circumstance. Among those who hastened to the spot to render assistance, we may mention a detachment of the Military-Officers and Men from the Steamship Mngdalena, Officers and Men from the Steamship Solent, Brand-Major Joseph Damel. CHRISTIAMSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 11th AUGUST, 1857. We learn from the St. Thomas Times of the 5th inst., that by the arrival of the Danish Schooner Pelegrina from Santo Domingo, via Porto Rico, further intelligence had been received of the insurrectionary movements in St. Domingo. President Baez had succeeded in quelling the demonstrations made at Scibo and the neighbouring districts. We copy below the proclamation issued by the President.

Proclamation of Buenaventura Baez, President of the Dominican Republic ! Dominicans ! The loyal troops arc following their march victoriously on the Eastern lines. The turbulents in sight of the expeditionary corps abandoned the point of San Jose de los Llanos, where they were encamped, and our forces entered it yesterday with (heir arms on their shouldieis at about 10 o'clock a. m. Meanwhile the Higuey corps, attacked by the Seibo on the evening of the 19th sustained a combat of an hour and a half, defeating the enemy, and causing them inexpressible loss : among them Colonel Blaz Maldonado, as well as various officers and soldiers fell. General Merced Marcano, a representative of Government in that community, could not have been more distinct in his details, than in those he gave of the action scarcely ended, before he explored the camp, to judge the importance of the triumph or victory. You see, then, Dominicans, that Divine- Providence þÿ protector of our just rights þÿ directs our operations ; He will undeceive the heedless, whose corrupted ambition has made them to apprehend that they were revolting against the Liberty and Religion of the State, which this Administration has known to respect more than any other. Never was the splendour of the Catholic worship, the dignity of the Priesthood, nor the rights of man, on a more solid basis than now in our native country. Dominicans ! I am satisfied with your patriotism, as also with the þÿ gation of the national corps, faithful sap- sublime abne-

porters of our national institutions, þÿ who do not cease in giving proofs of their devotedness and courage. Besides the great resources, Government depends upon your energy and upon tin; sanctity of your cause. The truth will remain splendidly proven, and society will find its equilibrium. Long live the Religion ! Long live the Dominican Republic! Long live the brave defen ders of Liberty ! National Palace, Santo Domingo, 2 1st, July, 1857, and 14th Year of Independence. BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.

TRINIDAD. The fourth Coolie vessel, the Scindian, has arrived with 232 more emigrants, making 1,316 adults received during the year. The latest arrival of Cape de Verde people are still under quarantine with the small pox. The amount of sugar shipped has reached 25,141 hhds. 4.430 tie- 4.069 brls. with 8,732 puns, and 323 trcs. of molasses, and ot cocoa, 3,549 366 lb. ; and there is shipping in the gulf to the amount of 5,600 tons ; from 7 dols 50 cts. to 8 dollars is the ruling rate for sugar here. The weather is very favourable, large quantities of rain fall, and yet every now and then we get a few hours fine breezy weather, which is both pleasant and eminently suited to promote vegetable growth. Labor to keep the weeds under is the one great want, and how to satisfy the demand for it is the great a problem for our Legislators to try and give solution to ; the Governor, at Council on the 1st, expressed a verv earnest desire that the Standing Committe r of immigration should bring up a report to let him know what has been done, and what farther can be done.

From the Jamaica Despatch.) The present state of the Sugar markets is probably the most remarkable that has occurred within modern experience. The value of Sugar has been forced up, ill the face of the most protracted money pressure that has been experienced for many years, to prices that would have been considered fabulous in 1851; and sucli is the present adjustment of demand and supply that there appears no immediate prospect of material change in the permanent value of this description of produce. Perhaps, however, there is no more important fact in relation to this question than the influence which the consumption of the United States has i xerci h and still continues to exercise, upon the Sugar markets of the world. Iu Europe, according to the accounts made up to the 1st May, the imports of Sugar iuto the principal ports of Great Britain and of the Continent to that date, exhibited a decrease as complied with hist year of above 15 0 ,0 ton-, the principal decrease being found to have occurred in English ports. On the other hand, the aggregate stocks in England and Europe shewed a deficiency on the 1st May of some 3J,00J tons, the entire deOoit being exhibited by the stocks ill English ports. It would -eem, therefore, that England lias ceased to he cons.dercd the best, market lot- Sugar, as it was a few years ago, and we must look elsewhere ill order to learn where the large quantity of produce of this year's crop lias been consigned. Nor have we far to go for this in-

formation The importations of Sugar iqto the United States, and particularly into the port of New-York, during the present year, have been of almost incredible magnitude. As an illustration of the extent to which this new and promi ing market has been glutted of late with this description of Colonial produce, we may stato that between Friday, the 22nd, and Sunday the 2d tli .May last, both days iuclusive, there were lauded in the port of New York from forty Jive vessels, no less than 14,291 hogsheads of Sugar, and this in addition to a stock already largely in excess of any former year. According to the latest advices received from New York the stock of Sugar at that port exceeded 60,060 hogsheads, besides molasses. It might be supposed that this enormous accumulation of Sugar at one point would have produced a necessarily large and immediate reaction in the value of the commodity, but there is this peculiarity in relation to the Sugar trade of New York, that by far the larger portion of the supply is iu the hands of speculators who have purchased at high prices and who cannot afford to throw it upon a falling market. The consequence is that notwithstanding the large supply, the markets are sparingly supplied, and prions are maintained. The greater portion of the Sugar now held in the United States is warehoused, awaiting the change of the duties which will come into operation on the 1st July. What effect the reduction of 6 per cent, iu the duties will have on prices remains to be seen ; but the

It is clear, from the figures we have given above, that importations iuto the United State.- cannot be very greatly increased f . some time to come without materially perilling the interest of those who already hold such large stocks ; and us the supply in England is now below the average consumption, and infinitely below the stocks held at corresponding period- for several years past, we may expect to hear of consul ruble shipments to London before long. Still it is an ascertained lact that the entire available supply of the year will be a deficient one, and that whatever the importations may be between this and the autumn, no such excess of supply can occur us will materially effect the value ol Sugar. SPAIN. The latest newspapers give details of the disturbances in the provinces. Some of these may be exaggerated, but the truth suffices to

inspires uneasiness. The town of Utrera, in Andalusia a place of 12,000 inhabitants, lias been entered by an insurgent force, varying in strengt i, according to different accounts, from 100 to 200 men. The town hud no military garrisoq; some enrnbmeros, Customhouse guards, þÿ þÿ who were there, took to flight, with their officer, one Paniagua; a handful of gendarmes defended themselves in their barracks until it was set on fire ; the insurgents, who all bad firearms of one sort or other, some of these being quite new, burned the archives of the Ayuntamiento, seized arms and horses, and levied on the town a contribution of G,500 dollars, which they took away with them. About 100 of the inhabitants of Utrera accompanied them when they departed, but some of these, with the proverbial fickleness of Andalusians, had already returned at the date of the last advices. Many of the insurgents proceeded from Seville; their device w.s Republican. They were chiefly artisans. Troops have been sent in their pursuit. The province of Seville lias been proclaimed in a state of siege. A newspaper speaks of a slight attempted disturbance at Logrono. Such reports, more or less well founded, arrive from all parts. It is said, with much appearance of truth, that these insurrectionary movements have been fomented, if not altogether got up, by the Spanish Democrats now refugees in Portugal. The Government is likely to take extraordinary measures, and perhaps the whole country, or a considerable portion of it, may be declared

under martial law. A telegraphic dispatch, dated Tuesday, says: þÿ "'lite sedition at Utrera lias been completely crushed. Twenty-nine of the rebel band were killed ; 22 others will expiate their crime."

INDIA. Letters have been received front Lahore, dated 14th, 15th, and 16th May. They represent the British at that station as being in a state of great excitement and anxiety, The troops were paraded on the 13th ; the sepoys were ordered to pile their arms, the cavalry to throw their swords on the ground and march to the rear; and, to the " astonishment and satisfaction of all the English," they obeyed. Their communication with the provinces beyond Umballa was cut off". Three hundred of the sepoys got off" to Ferozepore ; but they are said to have been punished by some Punjabees on the road. At Ferozepore the 10th Light Cavalry stuck to the British ; the 72nd Native Infantry laid down their arms ; the 45th were cut to pieces. The insurgents burned nine bungalows and a church ; but all the Europeans were " safe. The same letters men- tion that there were evident signs of mutiny at Umballa," though " all was quiet" at a later date.

The Governor of Java has received a copy of a very curious document, being a proclamation published by the Emperor of Japan, and undressed to all the maritime Powers, making known to them that he is ready to enter into treaties of commerce with them similar to those which he executed with Great Britain, France, the United .States, and Holland. This authentic document has been translated from the Japanese language into Dutch and French, and communicated to the European agents residing in the ports of China.

By the arrival of the Rosaline yesterday morning we received the painful intelligence of the demise, at St. Thomas, of the Rev. Mr. Baumann, Danish Lutheran Minister of that Island. It is truly lamentable, that the Community of St. Thomas has within so short a period been deprived of the services of two such valuable men as the late Rev. Baumann and his predecessor. There is a consideration, in connection with the death of these Ministers, which presses itself with some force on our minds. We allude to the almost unnecessary exposure to which the Lutheran clergyman in St. Thomas is subject by being obliged to cross the sea in an open boat, under the burning rays of a tropical sun, when on his way to hold Divine Service in the neighbouring Island, St. Johns. As far as we have been led to understand, the congregation, for whom these clergymen are obliged to expose their lives, can be counted by tens ; and in our opinion, its spiritual wants could well he supplied by one of the members of the Moravian church established in that Island. \\ e commend these remarks to the authorities, who, no doubt, will take every step within their power to avoid the sacritice of such valuable lives.

Mr. Marshman explained that the object of the deputation was to invite the attention of Her Majesty's Government to the question of a telegraphic communication with India, which, from the recent occurrences in that empire, had become a matter of the most urgent necessity. The a-sociation represented by this deputation projected the telegraph to India, via the Red Sea, two years ago, hut had remained in abeyance, after deputing an agent to obtain the necessary iiriuans from the Porte. Meanwhile another project was started for a telegraph to India down the Euphrates Valley, which the Treasury had encouraged by a conditional promise of 12,000/. per annum, and the East India Company had agreed, at a cost, assumed at from 200,000/. to 300,000/., to lay down a line in connexion with it from the head of the Per" sian Gulf to Kurrachee. If there had been any substantial progress made in the construction of that line during the last twelve-month, or if facilities had been increased for it, there

would have been less occasion for this deputation. But there had been no apparent advance, and it seemed improbable that it could be executed before the line of the contemplated railway was completed It was to run through a wild country, inhabited by barbarous tribes, ever at feud with each other, and beyond the control of their own rulers. The correspondent of the 'limes recently stated that the I anzimat at Constantinople refused to encourage this telegraphic line down the Euphrates, because the Turkish Government could not protect it. A submarine cable would he comparatively free from risk. The association having obtained the necessary firmans Irotn the Porte was now prepared to commence operations, on obtaining the necessary encouragement from Government and the East India Company, and to complete the line in 18 months. The object of the deputation was to press on Her Majesty's Government the urgency of the case, and to induce them to concentrate their efforts on that line which could be the most speedily constructed, and offeree the best chance of permanent security. His Lordship received the deputation with his accustomed courtesy, and, after making a number of inquiries on the subject, desired that a representation might be sent to him in writing, London Times, July 17. þÿ þÿ

The lecture was illustrated by the use of tabular diagrams. The chair was again taken by C. Gurney, Esq. Now it will 1 e endeavour to bring belore you this evening nij few of the salient facts and the chief , rineiples of taking science as applied to agriculture. On so large me to do more than touch a subject it would be perfectly impossible for order to parties upon a few points: and if at some subsequent period I should have the honour of again appearing before yon, the points which I leave unnoticed this evening may then form the subject-matter of another leciure (cheers). Allow ine in the first instance to point out to you what I have termed 11 the application of science to agriculture " Agriculture, as an art, has existed from t me immemorial Our fathers and our grandfathers

and our great-grandfathers, and all our ancestors before them, ploughed the land and liarrowed the land and tilled the land ; they obtained crops and realized certain results from certain operations þÿ in our country in one way, in another country in another way But the facts of their art, however numerous and important, had never been collected þÿ had been strung, as it were, together; they were never like the beads of a necklace, each unimportant by itself, but when strung together forming an important whole. Now the application of science to agriculture at the present time is to collect the facts of agriculture, facts with which you have become perfectly familiar in your own experience, and to show why certain causes produce certain effects ; and I believe I shall be able to point out to you somesome of the facts with which you are, your- thing to-night which will enable yoti to trace their selves acquainted, to certain simple and definite causes The first point to which I shall di- 1 absence of rect your attention is the nature of soils, because I think that before we commence any investigation into the nature of plants wo cessity should know something about the character of j ploughing, by harrowing, and by every other the soils in which they grow. Viewing our ! mechanical means that is planet as a whole, we may regard it as consisting of earth, or solid matter ; water, or liquid matter : and air, or gaseous matter. These three kinds of matter are quite capable of

changing their form. The solid may become a liquid or a gas, the gas a liquid or a solid ; and a liquid may become either the one or the other. 1 lie particular mode in which any of these forms of matter is presented to us depends upon heat ; so that, you see, the old myth of the ancient philosophers, that fire, air, earth, and water are the four elements, is not in reality so very far wrong. Taking a broad and general view , it may be affirmed that the solid matter, the liquid matter, and the gaseous matter, aided by the light and the heat of tlio situ which acts upon all these, are the great elements upon which the animal and the vege table existence of the whole world depends, Now in this country, (Cornwall) we arc blessed with a very large amount of a certaiiwrock called granite, which is regarded by geologists as the primitive rock of the world, containing within itself the material from which mo>t of the other rocks have been derived by action of some kind or other upon its surface. This granite, supposed to he the primeval rock, has been subjected to the operation of certain causes. Now granite rock consists of certain substances which are subject to the action of the air. Without mentioning at the present moment those properties of the air which act upon granite, let me point out to you that one of the chief ingredients in granite is feldspar, which is found in all the granite in Cornwall. This contains 65 per cent, of a substance called silica, which you know very well under the

name of sand. I am not speaking now of the shell-sand of the coast, but of hard, gritty, sili eious sand. It contains also 18 per cent, of a substance called alumina, which is the base of clay; a pine alumina is, in fact, a pure argil laceous matter. It also contains a substance called potash, to the extent of about. 15 per cent. Now nothing at first sight appears more indestructible than granite rock. But there is abundant evidence that granite is very destructible, especially if it contain a large amount ot f. ldspar. Porcelain clay, which is found in such large quantities in this country, is obtained from th, decomposition of granite, and what is called china-stone is simply granite partially decomposed. Now what is the. nature of the action of the air in this case ? There is a certain principle in the air called carbonic-acid gas, which acts upon the potash in the feldspar, and desolves it out ; and of course, the effect of dissolving the potash is just like that of the mortar out of a wall þÿ the otlior 111a terials fall to pieces. If in the. district of St. Austle did not wash out the clay iu use it for various artificial purposes, the rain which falls from heaven, and the conduce tinual action of the air, would eventually pro- the same result. And without entering into any description of other substances similar to feldspar, I would simply observe that the general origin of clay soils is the decomposition of substances containing alumina in quantities. \\ bile you find the alumina, which is very

light substance, washed down into one, part, you have the silicious matter washed down into another part ; and this disintegrating and washing process on different rocks goes on until you get every variety of soil that can be Conceived, from a clay to a sharp sand. Well, now, having seen that soils owe their primary origin directly to the disintegration of rocks, of which there is such an aliuudance in Cornwall, let us now proceed to consider the effect of atmospheric action upon soils themselves when they have been formed. Now, gentlemen, there arc certain substances in the soil, which are, as 1 have before intimated, soluble ; potash, soda, lime, magnesia, phosphate of lime, Ac., are some of them. These substaii res are continually acted upou in the soil by the air þÿ that is to say, they are liberated from insoluble combinations in a soluble form, provided the air acts upon thein ; while in the atmospheric action they are not rendered soluble. Thus we at once see the, neof exposing the land to the, air by
suitable, in order to secure the liberation of those substances which are essential to the growth of plants. (To be continued.)

By the arrival at St. Thomas of the Atrato we have received London Papers to the 3rd August. We make some extracts below in reference to Indian Affairs aud to China.

The alteration in the Upper Court proposed by Government during the Session ot the Colonial Council in 1S54 and which was recommended by a large majority will come into operation on the 1st September next. According to this regulation there will be but one Chief Justice who will alone decide all cases app' aled to the Upper Court. It remains yet to be seen whether this measure will be one of advantage to the Colonies in a juridical point of view. Pecuniary considerations, we are told, have led to it ; but whether the pruning knife should first have been applied to the Courts ot Justice in preference to the many other large items of expenditure, is a question in regard to which we must own ourselves open to conviction.
